title: Six hours
stance: The fit scores are taken as given. This plan does not try to max every path. The main line is trading risk, risk product, and risk platform. Two deep foundations sit beside that line without extending the calendar: Murex market & credit risk / risk technology, and tokenised / digital-asset institutional risk — both reuse the same 26 weeks with a different lens. AI risk, practiced as an AI engineer, is the first backup. Quant risk and multi-asset risk are the second backup. Prime brokerage / buy-side portfolio risk is a bridge that now includes portfolio construction, factor risk, hedging, portfolio stress, and PM interaction — mapped onto existing weeks, not extra calendar. Generic trading product stays a narrow slice. The professional moat this plan compounds is institutional market & credit risk × trading risk × digital assets × risk technology/product.
hardLimit: A five-year formal product-manager title cannot be manufactured in 156 hours. The substitute is the portfolio from weeks 5 to 8 and 24 to 26.
privacy: Use public documents and synthetic numbers. Do not put employer positions, client names, or live thresholds into the notebooks, the RAG index, or a public repository.

weeks.title: Option payoffs and the Greeks

sessions.text: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 11th ed., Ch. 10 (mechanics of options markets), Ch. 11 (properties of stock options), and the payoff diagrams in Ch. 12. Stop after you can price a position by payoff, not after the whole book. Core ideas: intrinsic versus time value, and put-call parity.

One-page Greek sheet. For a long at-the-money call and a short at-the-money put, write the sign of delta, gamma, vega, and theta. Then eight lines: what a short-gamma book does in a 10% gap, and which desk would feel it first.
Price a European call with S=100, K=100, r=0.02, sigma=0.20, T=0.5. Implement Black–Scholes twice, once with math.erf and once with scipy.stats.norm.cdf. Print price, delta, gamma, vega, and theta.
Write a list of 8 named people: 3 trading-risk managers, 3 risk product managers, 2 people who ship AI into a risk workflow. Firm, role, and why each person is on the list. Send nothing this week.

criteria: Greek sheet exists on one page, with signs for delta, gamma, vega, and theta on both positions, plus the 8-line gap note.
The two Black–Scholes implementations agree to 1e-6, and the notebook prints price, delta, gamma, vega, and theta.
The 8-person list is saved with a reason for each name. No pitch sent.
weeks.goal: Price a European call from first principles and state, with signs, what each Greek does to a long call and a short put when the market gaps.
weeks.bigIdea: An option payoff is the cash you get at expiry if you hold to maturity; the price you pay today is that payoff discounted and probability-weighted under a model. Greeks are the first sensitivities of that price: delta to the underlying, gamma to how delta itself moves, vega to volatility, and theta to the passage of time. For a risk desk, signs matter more than closed-form elegance: a short-gamma book that looks flat on delta can still explode when the spot gaps 10 percent overnight.

lessons.title: Payoff first, then price
body: Start with a European call: the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at a fixed strike K on a fixed expiry. At expiry the payoff is max(S − K, 0). A European put pays max(K − S, 0). Intrinsic value is that payoff if expiry were now; time value is the rest of the premium. You already know exchange liquidation paths; here the point is different: before any Greek or hedge, you must be able to draw the payoff diagram and state the cash at expiry for any terminal spot.

Put-call parity for European options on a non-dividend stock says C − P = S − K e^{−rT}. In words: a long call and short put equals a synthetic forward. If parity is broken after costs, arbitrage desks trade it; if it holds, you can still use it as a sanity check when a pricing library returns nonsense. For risk work, parity is a reconciliation tool: if your marked call and put imply a forward that disagrees with the listed future by more than the carry band, either the marks are stale or the inputs disagree.

Work a concrete book. Long one ATM call, short one ATM put, same strike and expiry, on a stock at 100. At expiry, if S = 110 the call pays 10 and the put expires worthless, so the combo pays +10. If S = 90 the call is worthless and the short put loses 10, so the combo pays −10. That is a forward-like payoff. Your risk question is not the diagram; it is which desk owns the residual if the options are American, the stock pays a dividend, or the borrow cost sits outside the model.

example.title: ATM call and put at expiry
example.story: Spot S = 100, strike K = 100, one European call bought for 5.80 and one European put sold for 4.90, both with T = 0.5 years left at trade time. At expiry, if S = 108 the call pays 8 and the put pays 0, so the combo cash at expiry is +8. Net of the initial premiums (paid 5.80, received 4.90), the realized P&L before financing is 8 − 5.80 + 4.90 = +7.10. If instead S = 94, the call pays 0 and the short put loses 6; P&L is −6 − 5.80 + 4.90 = −6.90. The shape is linear in S at expiry even though each leg is optional.
example.takeaway: If you cannot state expiry cash for a given terminal spot, you are not ready to talk about Greeks or hedges.

lessons.title: Greeks as signed risk, not trivia
body: Delta is the approximate change in option value for a one-unit change in the underlying. For a long call, delta is between 0 and 1; for a long put, between −1 and 0. Gamma is how fast delta changes when the underlying moves; long options have positive gamma, short options have negative gamma. Vega is sensitivity to a one-point move in volatility (convention varies; state your unit). Theta is the pull from time decay; long options usually have negative theta.

Signs for the two positions you will put on the Greek sheet: long ATM call — delta positive, gamma positive, vega positive, theta negative. Short ATM put — delta positive (short a negative-delta instrument), gamma negative, vega negative, theta positive. A book that is short both an ATM call and an ATM put is short gamma and short vega: calm markets drip theta income; a gap day forces you to chase delta at the worst prices.

Translate to a desk you already know. A market-making book that sells wings to earn premium is structurally short gamma. In a 10 percent overnight gap, delta jumps by roughly gamma times the move; hedges that assumed continuous rebalancing fail. The first pain is often the trading desk that must lift offers into a thin book, then the liquidation engine if margin calls cascade. Your eight-line note should name that path without citing any employer system.

example.title: Short gamma in a 10 percent gap
example.story: A short straddle on a stock at 100 has net delta ≈ 0, gamma ≈ −0.08 per one-point move (synthetic), and vega ≈ −0.25 per vol point. Spot gaps from 100 to 90. Rough delta after the gap is 0 + (−0.08) × (−10) ≈ +0.80 if gamma were constant — in reality gamma peaks near the strike so the true delta swing is larger. The desk must sell roughly 0.8 units of underlying per option to flatten, into a falling market. If 50,000 options are short, that is about 40,000 shares of forced selling. Vega also hurts if implied vol jumps from 20 percent to 35 percent: −0.25 × 15 × 50,000 is a large mark-to-market hit even before the delta hedge completes.
example.takeaway: Flat delta with short gamma is not a quiet book; it is a bet that the path stays continuous.

lessons.title: Black–Scholes as a calculator you can audit
body: Black–Scholes prices a European call as S N(d1) − K e^{−rT} N(d2), where N is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF): the probability that a standard normal random variable is less than or equal to a given number. You do not need the PDE derivation this week. You do need two independent CDF implementations that agree, because a silent wrong N(·) produces a silent wrong price and wrong Greeks. That is the same class of failure as two valuation engines disagreeing on a discount factor while both look internally consistent.

With S = 100, K = 100, r = 0.02, sigma = 0.20, T = 0.5, d1 and d2 are determined once; price, delta = N(d1), gamma, vega, and theta follow from the usual closed forms. Implement once with math.erf (the error function, a transform of the normal CDF) and once with scipy.stats.norm.cdf. Demand agreement to 1e-6 on every printed number. If they disagree, fix the helper before you trust any Greek sign on your sheet. Document vega and theta units in the notebook so a reviewer does not have to guess whether vega is per 1.00 or per 0.01 of volatility.

Optional deeper reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, chapters on option properties and the Black–Scholes formula. Stop when your notebook prints matching Greeks; do not turn the week into a PDE course. The deliverable is an audited calculator, not a derivation you will never retype in a risk review.

example.title: ATM half-year call inputs
example.story: Inputs: S = 100, K = 100, r = 0.02, sigma = 0.20, T = 0.5. Roughly, d1 ≈ 0.1414 and d2 ≈ 0.0000. The call price lands near 5.9 (order of magnitude check: ATM approx 0.4 S sigma sqrt(T) ≈ 0.4 × 100 × 0.20 × sqrt(0.5) ≈ 5.66, close enough before rates). Delta should be a bit above 0.5 because of the mild positive drift and the shape of N(d1). Gamma and vega peak near ATM; theta is negative for the long call. Your lab must print all five numbers from both CDF paths and show max abs difference below 1e-6.
example.takeaway: Two CDFs that agree beat one elegant formula you cannot prove matches production.

lab.goal: Implement Black–Scholes for a European call twice and print price, delta, gamma, vega, and theta with both CDF methods agreeing to 1e-6.
lab.why: Risk systems fail quietly when the normal CDF or day-count inputs disagree across libraries; proving two paths match is the skill, not memorizing the formula.
steps: Create a notebook or script. Import math and, if available, scipy.stats. Define inputs exactly: S=100, K=100, r=0.02, sigma=0.20, T=0.5.

Write a helper N_erf(x) = 0.5 * (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0))). Write N_scipy(x) = scipy.stats.norm.cdf(x). If scipy is missing, install it or use only erf for development, but the deliverable needs both.
Compute d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r + 0.5*sigma**2)*T) / (sigma*sqrt(T)) and d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T).

Call price: S*N(d1) - K*exp(-r*T)*N(d2). Delta: N(d1). Gamma: exp(-0.5*d1**2)/sqrt(2*pi) / (S*sigma*sqrt(T)). Vega: S * same normal density * sqrt(T) (report as sensitivity to 1.0 in sigma, or to 0.01 if you document that choice). Theta for a call: use the standard formula including the rate term on the strike; state the unit as value per year.
Run the full Greek set with N_erf and again with N_scipy. Print both blocks. Assert abs differences on price and each Greek are < 1e-6.
Optional check: ATM approximation 0.4*S*sigma*sqrt(T) should be within about 0.5 of your call price for these inputs.
expected: Printed call price near 5.9 from both methods, matching to 1e-6.
Printed delta, gamma, vega, theta from both methods, each pair agreeing to 1e-6.
Clear comment in the notebook stating vega and theta units.

weeks.title: Basis, futures hedge, and EWMA volatility

sessions.text: Hull 11th ed. Ch. 3 (hedging with futures and basis risk) and Ch. 5 (forward and futures prices: contango, backwardation, cost of carry). Then Ch. 15.4 and 15.11 only: what volatility means, and implied volatility. Skip the Black–Scholes PDE derivation.

On 60 daily returns (public prices are fine), compute 20-day realized volatility and RiskMetrics EWMA with lambda 0.94. Print both on the same dates.
Send two notes of at most five sentences. Each note contains one observation from week 1 and one specific question. No CV attached. Log the person and the date.

criteria: Basis memo states the formula, a numeric hedge ratio, and one cascade failure mode.
EWMA and 20-day realized volatility are printed for the same 60-day series.

weeks.goal: Define basis and a one-week futures hedge ratio for a market you can observe publicly, and compute realized versus EWMA volatility on the same return series.
weeks.bigIdea: Basis is the difference between the futures (or perpetual) price and the spot price you actually need to hedge; hedge ratios that ignore basis assume the two move one-for-one, which fails in stress. Contango means futures above spot; backwardation means futures below spot; cost of carry links fair forward to financing and storage. Realized volatility looks backward over a window; EWMA volatility (exponentially weighted moving average) weights recent returns more heavily so a shock shows up faster than a long equally weighted window.

lessons.title: Basis is the hedge error you can name
body: If you hedge a spot inventory with a futures contract, you care about F − S (or S − F; pick a convention and keep it). That difference is the basis. A textbook minimum-variance hedge ratio is h* = ρ σ_S / σ_F, where ρ is the correlation between spot and futures returns and σ are the volatilities. For a one-week horizon, estimate those from weekly returns, not from a five-year daily sample you never re-check.

In crypto perpetuals, the analogous object is often perp price versus index or spot, plus a funding rate that pulls the perp toward the index. You can observe BTC perp versus spot on a public venue without any internal data. Write the basis formula you will use in the memo, the numeric hedge ratio for a one-week horizon, and the assumption that dies in a liquidation cascade: usually stable correlation, continuous liquidity, or the idea that you can roll the hedge at yesterday’s bid-ask.

Cost of carry says a fair forward is roughly spot grown at financing minus benefits of holding the asset. Contango often appears when carry is positive and inventory is ample; backwardation can appear when the market pays up for spot. You do not need a full term-structure model this week; you need to say whether your observed basis is a carry story or a stress story.

example.title: One-week BTC perp hedge ratio
example.story: Spot BTC index at 60,000; perpetual at 60,180; basis = 180 dollars or 30 basis points (a basis point is 0.01 percent). Over the last 20 weeks, weekly spot vol σ_S = 8.0 percent, perp vol σ_F = 8.4 percent, correlation ρ = 0.97. Hedge ratio h* = 0.97 × 8.0 / 8.4 ≈ 0.92. So a 100 BTC spot long hedges with about 92 BTC of short perps for a one-week variance-minimum target. In a liquidation cascade, ρ can fall to 0.80 while σ_F jumps to 14 percent; the same formula then gives h* ≈ 0.46, and yesterday’s 0.92 hedge is the wrong size.
example.takeaway: State the ratio and the cascade assumption that invalidates it; a ratio without a failure mode is decoration.

lessons.title: Futures hedges and what 'flat' really means
body: A futures hedge makes you flat to the common factor only if the contract multiplier, currency, and delivery map to your exposure. Equity index futures versus a single-stock book leave idiosyncratic risk. Cross-margined crypto books leave coin-specific jumps. Your memo should name the residual in plain English: what still moves P&L after the hedge is on. If you cannot name the residual, you have described a trade, not a hedge, and the hedge ratio is marketing.

Stack-and-roll risk matters when the hedge expires before the exposure. You sell the near contract, buy it back, sell the next: each roll crystallizes basis. In calm markets rolls cost a few basis points; in stress the calendar spread widens as everyone rolls the same way. For a one-week horizon you may avoid the roll — say so explicitly if that is why you chose the contract and the expiry month.

For risk product work later in the plan, this week’s skill is specifying the hedge as a control: metric (basis or residual), horizon (one week), owner (desk), and failure mode (cascade correlation break). That is the same shape as a threshold memo in week 4. Practice writing the control sentence now so week 4 is refinement, not invention. Keep employer playbooks out; public markets only.

example.title: Index future versus stock basket
example.story: A 50 million dollar long basket of 20 stocks is hedged with E-mini notionals. Basket weekly vol 2.5 percent, future weekly vol 2.2 percent, correlation 0.90. Hedge ratio 0.90 × 2.5 / 2.2 ≈ 1.02, so about 51 million of short futures. In a week where one name gaps −30 percent on news while the index is −2 percent, the futures hedge offsets the index piece but the name-specific loss remains. Residual P&L ≈ 0.05 × 50m × (−0.30) if that name was 5 percent of the book: about −750,000 dollars unhedged.
example.takeaway: Hedge ratios cancel the factor you measured; they do not cancel the risks you excluded from the regression.

lessons.title: Realized vol versus EWMA
body: Realized volatility over 20 trading days is usually the sample standard deviation of daily returns, annualized by sqrt(252) if you report an annual number. Equally weighted windows are slow: a crash on day 0 still shares weight with day −19. EWMA variance with lambda 0.94 — the classic RiskMetrics daily choice — updates as variance_t = lambda * variance_{t-1} + (1-lambda) * r_t^2. Half-life is about ln(0.5)/ln(lambda) ≈ 11 days, so recent shocks dominate. Print both series on the same dates.

Implied volatility is the sigma you plug into a pricing model to match a market option price; it is a forecast embedded in prices, not a historical statistic. This week’s lab stays on historical measures. When you later set alerts, decide whether the control cares about realized, EWMA, or implied — they answer different questions and they will disagree on the day you need them most.

Build the lab so a second reader can rerun it: document lambda 0.94, the annualization factor, how you initialized EWMA, and whether sample variance uses ddof=1. Optional Hull sections on volatility are fine after the table prints. Your deliverable is the aligned series and one highlighted shock day, not a research paper on estimators. Label the shock row in the printed table.

example.title: Shock day: 20-day vs lambda 0.94
example.story: Fifty-nine quiet days with daily returns near ±0.5 percent, then day 60 returns −4.0 percent. A 20-day realized vol that includes the shock rises from about 8 percent annualized to roughly 14 percent depending on the quiet sample. EWMA with λ = 0.94, if it was sitting near 8 percent annualized, jumps more sharply because 6 percent of the new variance estimate is the fresh r² and the quiet history is discounted. On a chart aligned by date, EWMA turns first; 20-day realized follows as the shock rolls through the window.
example.takeaway: EWMA is a faster thermometer; realized is a slower average — pick the one that matches the decision latency of the control.

lab.goal: On 60 daily returns, compute 20-day realized volatility and RiskMetrics EWMA with lambda 0.94, printed on the same dates.
lab.why: You need a reproducible volatility pair before you defend any vol-based threshold or hedge ratio in later weeks.
steps: Obtain 61 consecutive daily closes for a public series (equity index or BTC). Compute 60 log returns r_t = ln(P_t / P_{t-1}).
For each t from 20 to 60, compute 20-day realized variance as the sample variance of r_{t-19}…r_t (state whether you use ddof=1). Annualize vol as sqrt(variance * 252). Record the date of day t.
Initialize EWMA variance. Practical approach: set σ²_0 to the sample variance of the first 20 returns, then for t = 21…60 update σ²_t = 0.94 * σ²_{t-1} + 0.06 * r_t**2. Annualize sqrt(σ²_t * 252).
Align the two series on dates where both exist. Print a table: date, r_t, realized_20d, ewma_0.94.
Sanity check: after a large |r_t|, ewma should move more than realized on that same day.
Optional deeper reading: Hull chapters on futures hedging and volatility; not required to finish the lab.
expected: A printed table with at least ~40 overlapping dates showing both vols.
Lambda documented as 0.94 and annualization factor documented as 252 (or another factor you justify).
One highlighted row where EWMA reacts faster than 20-day realized after a spike.

weeks.title: Margin tiers, haircuts, and liquidation

sessions.text: Read OKX public docs end to end for one path: tiered maintenance margin, isolated versus cross, and adjusted equity after collateral discounts (the v5 fields adjEq, mmr, and mgnRatio). Write five lines on how this differs from the liquidation and ADL path you already know from exchange trading risk.

Build a 6-row tier table for a hypothetical perpetual: notional band, maintenance margin rate, max leverage, and liquidation buffer. Under the top tier, write one sentence of the form: this tier exists because a clip of size X cannot be closed inside Y bps without moving the book.

Equity 100, position notional 500, maintenance margin rate 2%. Compute the margin ratio and the price move that reaches liquidation. Repeat for a two-asset cross book where asset B has a 10% collateral haircut. Show the arithmetic.
Leave one substantive public comment on a risk or product post. The comment must add a distinction, not praise. Log the URL.

criteria: Tier table has 6 rows and a written reason for the top tier that mentions exit capacity.
Isolated liquidation move and the haircut-adjusted cross case are both computed by hand, with formulas visible.
One public comment URL is logged.
weeks.goal: Compute liquidation distance for an isolated position and for a cross book with a collateral haircut, and explain why maintenance tiers widen with notional.
weeks.bigIdea: Maintenance margin is the equity you must keep against a position; below it the venue can liquidate. Isolated margin confines risk to one position’s assigned equity; cross margin shares equity across positions, which helps small moves and hurts when correlations jump to one. A haircut discounts collateral value so that 100 of coin B may count as only 90 of adjusted equity. Tiered maintenance rates rise with notional because exit capacity is finite: large clips cannot close inside a tight band without moving the book.

lessons.title: Margin ratio and the path to liquidation
body: Define equity as the account value available to absorb losses (cash plus unrealized P&L, under the venue’s rules). Position notional is the absolute exposure size, often |price × size|. Maintenance margin requirement (MMR) is a rate times notional, sometimes plus fixed fees. A common margin ratio is equity divided by notional, compared against MMR; when equity falls to the maintenance requirement, liquidation begins. Public OKX-style fields you may see discussed openly include adjusted equity, MMR, and margin ratio — read one public path end to end this week.

Work the lab numbers in your head: equity 100, notional 500, MMR 2 percent. Maintenance requirement = 0.02 × 500 = 10. Margin ratio = 100 / 500 = 20 percent, which is above 2 percent, so you are not at liquidation. The loss that takes equity from 100 down to 10 is 90. Relative to notional 500 that is an 18 percent adverse move on the position if one-for-one with price (details depend on side and contract multiplier; state your assumption).

Your study note should contrast this mechanical path with the liquidation and auto-deleveraging path you already know from exchange trading risk: who takes the other side, what price band is used, and what happens if the book cannot absorb the clip.

example.title: Isolated MMR arithmetic
example.story: Equity E = 100, notional N = 500, maintenance rate m = 2%. Maintenance requirement = 10. Current margin ratio E/N = 20%. Adverse P&L to hit maintenance = E − mN = 90. If a long linear position loses dollar-for-dollar with a spot decline, the liquidation move is 90/500 = 18% down. If the mark gaps 20% in one print, equity would go to 100 − 0.20×500 = 0, past maintenance, and liquidation should have triggered along the way under continuous marks — in practice marks jump, so the engine’s next mark is the event that matters.
example.takeaway: Always show maintenance requirement, margin ratio, and the price move that exhausts the buffer — three numbers, not one ratio in isolation.

lessons.title: Cross margin and haircuts
body: In cross mode, equity is shared. That raises capacity for uncorrelated books and creates hidden concentration when everything sells together. Adjusted equity applies haircuts: if asset B has a 10 percent haircut, only 90 percent of its mark counts. A two-asset example: asset A is the position; asset B is collateral. If you pretend haircuts are zero, you overstate the buffer and understate liquidation risk.

Repeat the lab with a haircut. Suppose equity is composed of 40 in cash-like collateral and 60 in asset B marked at full value, but B has a 10 percent haircut. Adjusted equity = 40 + 0.9×60 = 94. With notional 500 and MMR 2 percent, buffer to maintenance is 94 − 10 = 84, so the adverse move on the position is 84/500 = 16.8 percent, tighter than the 18 percent unhaircut case with equity 100. The point is the direction: haircuts shrink the fuse.

Write five lines on how this public mechanics story differs from the venue path you already operate: naming differences in adjusted equity, partial liquidation, and insurance-fund or ADL steps is enough. No internal parameters.

example.title: Ten percent haircut on collateral B
example.story: Cash collateral 40, coin B quantity worth 60 at last mark, haircut 10%, so adjEq = 40 + 54 = 94. Position notional 500, MMR 2%, maintenance = 10. Margin ratio on adjusted equity = 94/500 = 18.8%. Buffer = 84. Compared with treating B at full 60 (equity 100), you lost 6 of buffer solely from the haircut policy. If B’s mark also falls 10 percent in the same stress that hits the position, adjEq falls again: B contribution becomes 0.9 × 54 = 48.6 if the haircut still applies to the new mark — read the public rule; do not invent a venue’s compounding order without a citation.
example.takeaway: Cross margin without haircut math is fiction; adjusted equity is the number that pays the MMR bill.

lessons.title: Why tiers exist: exit capacity
body: Tier tables raise maintenance rates and cut max leverage as notional grows. The economic reason is exit capacity: a 50,000 dollar clip might exit inside 5 basis points; a 50 million dollar clip may need 40 basis points and still leave a tail. If MMR stayed flat, large accounts would run leverage the book cannot safely unwind. That is why the top tier exists — not because a committee liked round numbers on a slide.

Build a six-row tier table for a hypothetical perpetual: notional band, maintenance margin rate, max leverage, and liquidation buffer (define buffer once, then use it consistently). Under the top tier, write one sentence of the form: this tier exists because a clip of size X cannot be closed inside Y bps without moving the book. If that sentence is missing, the table is decoration for a design review and will not survive a markets question.

Tie this to capital thinking without dragging in a full FRTB pack: size-aware charges and liquidity horizons exist because markets are not infinitely deep. Your tier sentence is the trading-risk version of that idea. Keep the table synthetic and portable; it is a portfolio artifact, not a venue proposal you are asking anyone to ship next quarter.

example.title: Top tier justified by exit capacity
example.story: Tiers (notional → MMR → max leverage): 0–100k at 0.5%/50x; 100k–500k at 1%/25x; 500k–2m at 2%/20x; 2m–10m at 4%/10x; 10m–50m at 7%/5x; above 50m at 12%/3x. Top tier sentence: this tier exists because a clip of size 50 million cannot be closed inside 35 bps without moving the book, so maintenance equity must be thick enough to survive a wider liquidation band. Liquidation buffer from 3x initial leverage (about 33% initial margin) down to 12% MMR is roughly 21 percentage points of notional — the room the engine has before forced action.
example.takeaway: If the top tier lacks an exit-capacity sentence, the table is just numbers without a reason.

lab.goal: Compute margin ratio and liquidation move for equity 100 / notional 500 / MMR 2%, then repeat for a cross book with a 10% haircut on asset B.
lab.why: Hand arithmetic makes tier debates concrete; you cannot outsource the buffer calculation if you own the control.
steps: Isolated-style case: set E=100, N=500, m=0.02. Compute maintenance = m*N, margin ratio = E/N, buffer = E − maintenance, liquidation move ≈ buffer/N. Write each line.
Cross haircut case: split equity into A_cash=40 and B_mark=60 with haircut h=0.10. adjEq = 40 + (1-h)*60. Recompute margin ratio, buffer, and liquidation move using adjEq instead of E.
State assumptions: linear P&L with mark, one position, no fees, no partial liquidation ladder.
Optional: add a 5 bps fee on liquidation and show how the required buffer grows.
Compare to one public OKX (or similar) doc path for adjEq / mmr / mgnRatio naming; write five lines on differences versus the liquidation/ADL path you already know.
expected: Isolated: maintenance 10, ratio 20%, move 18% (under the linear assumption).
Haircut cross: adjEq 94, tighter buffer and move than the unhaircut case, arithmetic shown.
Assumptions listed so a reviewer can reproduce the numbers.

weeks.title: Why this threshold is 5% and not 3%

sessions.text: Hull 11th ed. Ch. 22.1–22.2 only: the definitions of VaR and expected shortfall. Then draft, from memory, the four costs of a bad threshold: missed loss, false positives, time to react, and who owns the decision.

Threshold memo, at most 700 words, for one control you can describe without confidential numbers (abnormal price, concentration, or liquidation buffer). Required headings: decision, metric definition, loss if the band is too wide, alert volume if the band is too tight, owner, evidence that would change the number, rollback.
Ten-line risk finding written to a Head of Risk. Include current exposure, the limit you recommend, and the exact decision you need. Use synthetic numbers.
Ask one person on the week-1 list for a 20-minute conversation in the next six weeks. One ask. Log it.

criteria: Memo contains both a loss argument and a false-positive argument, plus an owner and a rollback.
The 10-line finding asks for one explicit decision.
One meeting request is sent and logged.
weeks.goal: Defend a single control threshold with both a loss argument and a false-positive argument, name an owner, and ask a Head of Risk for one explicit decision.
weeks.bigIdea: A threshold is a product decision dressed as a number: set it wide and you miss loss; set it tight and you drown the desk in false positives. Value at Risk (VaR) is a loss quantile over a horizon and confidence level; expected shortfall is the average loss beyond that quantile — useful vocabulary, not the whole memo. The four costs of a bad threshold are missed loss, false alerts, slow reaction, and unclear ownership. Your job this week is to write the memo that makes 5 percent versus 3 percent a reasoned choice, not a tribal preference.

lessons.title: VaR and expected shortfall as language for tails
body: VaR answers: how bad can it get at a chosen confidence over a chosen horizon, as a single cutoff. Expected shortfall answers: given we are past that cutoff, what is the average loss. For threshold design on operational controls — abnormal price, concentration, liquidation buffer — you rarely paste regulatory VaR into the alert engine. You still need the mindset: name the loss metric, the horizon, and the tolerance for missing events. Optional reading: Hull on VaR and expected shortfall definitions only.

Draft from memory the four costs of a bad threshold: missed loss when the band is too wide; false positives when the band is too tight; time to react when detection is slow or noisy; and who owns the decision when the number must change. If any of the four is missing from a threshold debate, the debate is incomplete. Write them on a card before you open the memo template so you do not skip ownership under time pressure.

Connect this to week 3’s fuse length. A liquidation-buffer alert at 3 percent of notional versus 5 percent is the same tradeoff as a VaR limit that is tight or loose: you are buying earlier information with more noise, or calm inboxes with later information. Make that tradeoff numeric in the memo, even if the dollars are synthetic. Synthetic and explicit beats vague and confidential every time.

example.title: 3% versus 5% concentration alert
example.story: Control: alert when one name’s share of account equity exceeds a threshold. At 3%, historical synthetic books of 1,000 accounts show 120 alerts/day, of which analysts dismiss 95 as known market-making inventory. At 5%, alerts fall to 28/day and dismissals fall to 10, but a post-mortem shows two accounts that later lost 15% of equity from a single-name gap would have alerted at 3% two hours earlier and at 5% only after the move had begun. Missed-loss estimate: 2 accounts × 2 hours × average 50k per hour of preventable add-on risk = 200k synthetic. False-positive cost at 3%: roughly 95 × 4 minutes × fully loaded 1.5$/minute ≈ 570$/day of analyst time, plus alert fatigue.
example.takeaway: Pick 5% only if you write down the missed-loss story and the fatigue story; otherwise the number is fashion.

lessons.title: Structure of a threshold memo that survives review
body: Required headings: decision; metric definition; loss if the band is too wide; alert volume if the band is too tight; owner; evidence that would change the number; rollback. Cap at 700 words. Use a control you can describe without confidential numbers: abnormal price move, concentration, or liquidation buffer. If a heading is empty, the memo is not done — shorten elsewhere, do not drop the heading to save space.

Metric definition must be reproducible: field names in plain English, window length, and filters such as exclude new listings under 48 hours. Loss if too wide needs a scenario with dollars, even if synthetic. Alert volume if too tight needs a count per day and who pays the time. Owner is a role, not the system. Rollback is the prior number plus the condition that triggers revert — not a vague promise to monitor after launch.

Write the memo as if a skeptical Head of Risk will skim it in four minutes. Lead with the decision sentence. Put the 3 percent versus 5 percent contrast in one table. Park theory in a single short paragraph. The finding in the next lesson will steal from this memo; keep the numbers consistent across both artifacts so you are not running two different stories.

example.title: Liquidation-buffer threshold memo sketch
example.story: Decision: alert when buffer-to-maintenance falls below 5% of notional, not 3%. Metric: (adjEq − maintenance) / notional using haircut-adjusted equity. Loss if too wide: in a synthetic replay, accounts between 3% and 5% buffer contributed 1.2m of liquidation shortfall over 90 days when marks gapped. Alert volume if too tight: 3% threshold produces ~400 alerts/day versus ~90 at 5% on the same synthetic book; desk capacity is ~120 serious investigations/day. Owner: Head of Trading Risk for the asset class. Evidence to change: if shortfall from the 3–5% bucket exceeds 500k in a rolling 30 days, revisit. Rollback: revert to 3% within one config publish if false-negative loss exceeds 500k in a week.
example.takeaway: A threshold memo without rollback and owner is an opinion piece.

lessons.title: The ten-line finding that asks for a decision
body: Executives do not need your full memo in the finding. They need current exposure, the limit you recommend, and the exact decision. Ten lines to a Head of Risk. Synthetic numbers only. End with a yes/no or choose-A/B ask. If line 10 is happy to discuss, you failed the exercise — rewrite until the ask is a decision someone can make in a meeting without another deck.

Avoid stacking jargon. If you must say expected shortfall, define it in one line as average loss past the cutoff. Prefer cash and counts over model names. Reuse the memo’s dollars so you are not running two parallel stories. This finding is also practice for industry conversations: clear asks travel better than background essays that bury the request in context.

After you draft, cut any line that does not change the decision. Current threshold, proposed threshold, missed-loss cost, false-positive cost, owner, rollback, shadow period, and the ask almost always earn a line. History of how you felt about 3 percent last year almost never does. Print it, read it aloud in under 90 seconds, and fix where you stumble. Put a Friday decision date on line 10.

example.title: Finding with a binary ask
example.story: Lines: (1) Scope: perpetual concentration control, synthetic book. (2) Current threshold 3% of equity in one name. (3) Current alert load 120/day, ~80% closed as inventory. (4) Proposed threshold 5%. (5) Replay: missed early warning on 2 accounts with 200k preventable add-on risk. (6) Benefit: alerts to 28/day, inside desk capacity. (7) Owner after change: Trading Risk Manager, liquid markets. (8) Rollback: return to 3% if a single-name loss >100k occurs without a prior 5% alert. (9) Evidence window: 30 trading days shadow. (10) Decision needed by Friday: approve 5% with shadow, keep 3%, or commission a different metric.
example.takeaway: Line 10 must be a decision, not a request for more analysis alone.

lab.goal: Draft the quantitative skeleton behind a 5% versus 3% choice using synthetic alert counts and loss estimates you invent consistently.
lab.why: The memo’s numbers must come from a worksheet you can defend, even when the data is synthetic.
steps: Choose one control: abnormal price, concentration, or liquidation buffer.
Invent a synthetic population: e.g. 1,000 accounts, 30 days.
At threshold 3% and 5%, assign alert counts/day and a count of 'true' events (define true in one sentence).
Compute false-positive rate ≈ (alerts − true)/alerts and a missed-loss dollars figure for the wider band.
Write the seven memo headings in outline form with those numbers filled in.
Draft the ten-line Head of Risk finding ending in one explicit decision.
expected: A small table with 3% vs 5% alert volume, true events, and loss/fatigue estimates.
Memo outline with all required headings populated.
Ten-line finding whose last line is a clear decision request.

weeks.title: Own one slice: problem, non-goals, acceptance tests

sessions.text: Read Marty Cagan’s writing on product discovery versus delivery (Inspired, the discovery chapters, or the SVPG article Product Discovery at svpg.com/product-discovery). Extract only this distinction: what you must learn before you write requirements.

One-page roadmap for a single risk-control slice you could own. Required: problem, user (risk officer, trader, or engineer), three outcomes, explicit non-goals, and two risks to the slice. If it does not fit on one page, cut scope, not font size.
Five acceptance tests in Given / When / Then. A tester who has not spoken to you must be able to mark each one pass or fail.
Send the problem statement, not the solution, to one engineer and one trader. Ask what you got wrong. Log both replies, including silence after a reasonable wait.

criteria: Roadmap is one page and names at least one non-goal.
Five Given / When / Then tests are writable as pass or fail without you in the room.
Two people were asked what is wrong with the problem statement, and the replies are logged.
weeks.goal: Own one risk-control slice as a product: problem, user, outcomes, non-goals, and five acceptance tests a stranger can pass/fail.
weeks.bigIdea: Discovery is learning what must be true before you write requirements; delivery is building once those truths are stable enough. A risk product slice is not a feature laundry list — it is a problem, a user, three outcomes, and explicit non-goals. Acceptance tests in Given / When / Then form turn arguments into binary checks. If a tester who has not spoken to you cannot mark pass or fail, you do not yet have a product definition.

lessons.title: Discovery before requirements
body: Marty Cagan’s product discovery versus delivery distinction is simple: discovery asks whether you are building the right thing for the right user; delivery asks whether you can ship it reliably. In risk, right means the control changes a decision under time pressure — a risk officer stops an add, a trader reduces size, an engineer pages on a broken mark — not that a dashboard looks busy. Read the discovery chapters or the SVPG Product Discovery article and extract only that distinction.

List what you must learn before requirements. Typical unknowns: who is interrupted by the alert; what action they take within 15 minutes; what data field is missing today; what you will not automate. Write those unknowns down before you draft tickets. If the list is empty, you are guessing. Prefer two interviews and one payload inspection over ten stories written from imagination alone.

Your week-4 threshold work feeds this slice. Reuse the same control so the portfolio compounds instead of resetting. The problem statement you will send to an engineer and a trader this week should contain no solution architecture — only the decision someone cannot make today and why that costs money or time. Silence after five days is a data point: the problem may not be compelling as written.

example.title: Unknowns before writing tickets
example.story: Proposed slice: concentration early-warning for perpetual accounts. Unknowns listed before requirements: (1) Does the night risk officer or the desk head acknowledge alerts? (2) Is the action 'raise MMR', 'cut API limit', or 'call the client'? (3) Is adjusted equity available with haircuts in the alert payload today, or only raw equity? (4) Non-goal candidate: no auto-liquidation from this slice. Learning plan: two interviews, one payload inspection on synthetic fixtures, one shadow count of alerts at 5%. Only after that do you write stories.
example.takeaway: If you cannot list the unknowns, you are already writing requirements too early.

lessons.title: One-page roadmap: cut scope, not font size
body: Required on one page: problem; user (risk officer, trader, or engineer); three outcomes; explicit non-goals; two risks to the slice. Outcomes are changes in the world — false positives under 20 per day, median time to ack under 10 minutes — not modules like build a streaming pipeline. If it does not fit on one page, cut scope. Shrinking the font is cheating and reviewers notice immediately.

Non-goals protect you from polite scope creep. Examples: not replacing the liquidation engine; not providing regulatory capital numbers; not supporting options until the perpetual path is stable. Write non-goals as firmly as outcomes. Stakeholders argue with what you wrote; they cannot argue with what you only thought and never put on the page.

Risks to the slice are delivery and adoption risks: missing haircut fields; desk ignores alerts; legal blocks client contact scripts. Name them so the argument happens early. Carry forward week 4’s owner and rollback ideas — a slice without an owner is a science project. Keep the page free of employer secrets; synthetic metrics are fine. Hand the page to someone else and ask them to restate the user and one non-goal.

example.title: One-page slice that fits
example.story: Problem: night officers learn concentration only after maintenance ratio alerts, average 40 minutes late on synthetic review. User: night risk officer. Outcomes: (1) alert when single-name share >5% of adjEq; (2) median ack <10 minutes; (3) false positives <20/day after week 4. Non-goals: no auto-trading, no capital model, no UI redesign beyond the existing alert inbox. Risks: adjEq field incomplete on 8% of accounts; officers snooze all alerts during CPI releases. Page count: one.
example.takeaway: If it needs a second page, you have two slices — pick one.

lessons.title: Acceptance tests strangers can grade
body: Write five tests as Given / When / Then. Given is the fixture; When is the event; Then is the observable result. Avoid should be reasonable. Prefer emits AlertEvent with code CONC_5 and account_id X. A tester with only the fixtures and the five lines should grade without Slack access to you. If they must ask what you meant, rewrite Then until it is binary and checkable from data alone.

Include at least one negative test: a case that must not alert. Include one haircut or data-quality case if your slice depends on adjusted equity. Include a cooldown or dedup case if duplicate alerts are a known failure mode. These negative and edge tests are where risk products usually break in week one of production, not in the happy-path demo.

Map each test to an outcome on the one-pager so you are not testing trivia. If an outcome has zero tests, either drop the outcome or add a test. Save the five tests next to the roadmap; weeks 6 and 8 will quote them when metrics and replay need a definition of true alert. Freeze the five tests before you invent week-6 formulas.

example.title: Five Given/When/Then tests
example.story: (1) Given account A with adjEq 1,000,000 and name BTC at 60,000 (6%), when marks refresh, then alert CONC_5 fires once. (2) Given account B with BTC at 4%, when marks refresh, then no CONC_5 alert. (3) Given account C with raw equity 1,000,000 but adjEq 800,000 after haircuts and BTC notional 45,000 (5.625% of adjEq), when marks refresh, then alert fires using adjEq not raw equity. (4) Given account A already alerted in the last 30 minutes, when marks refresh with still 6%, then no duplicate alert (cooldown). (5) Given missing adjEq field, when marks refresh, then data-quality alert DQ_ADJEQ fires and CONC_5 does not silently use raw equity.
example.takeaway: If a test needs you to interpret 'makes sense', rewrite Then until it is binary.

weeks.title: Metrics that move after launch

sessions.text: Read one metrics frame and apply it to an internal tool, not a consumer app. Use the HEART framework’s task-success and adoption parts, or the one-metric chapter of Lean Analytics. Ignore vanity launch metrics.

Metric dictionary for the week-5 slice. Six rows: false-positive rate, incident rate, detection coverage, manual minutes per case, loss exposure, decision latency. Each row needs a formula, a source, a baseline you will measure, and a 90-day target.
Mark two metrics computable from data you already have, and two that are blocked. For the blocked pair, name the missing field.
Show the dictionary to one risk colleague. Ask them to delete one metric. Record which one and why.

criteria: Six metrics each have a formula, a source, a baseline, and a 90-day target.
Two metrics are marked computable now, and two blocked metrics name the missing field.
One colleague has argued for deleting a metric, and that argument is written down.
weeks.goal: Publish a six-metric dictionary for the week-5 slice with formulas, sources, baselines, and 90-day targets, and mark what is computable now versus blocked.
weeks.bigIdea: After launch, vanity counts (alerts sent, dashboards opened) flatter you without proving the control works. Useful metrics for an internal risk tool track task success and adoption: did the officer make the right decision faster, with fewer false interrupts, and less loss. A metric dictionary row is incomplete without formula, source, baseline, and target. Blocked metrics must name the missing field — 'we should track loss' without a join key is not a metric, it is a wish.

lessons.title: Task success beats launch vanity
body: HEART-style framing (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success) is built for consumer products; for internal risk tools, steal task success and adoption and ignore consumer happiness theater. Lean Analytics’ one-metric idea helps only if that metric can move from a decision you own. Prefer a short dictionary of six honest metrics over one glamorous north star you cannot compute. Ignore vanity launch metrics such as alerts emitted with no disposition attached.

The six required rows are false-positive rate, incident rate, detection coverage, manual minutes per case, loss exposure, and decision latency. Each needs a formula a data person could implement without a meeting. Baseline is what you measure before claiming victory — even if the baseline is not measured yet, sample starts Monday. Targets are numeric and dated, not adjectives like better or healthier.

Tie each metric back to a week-5 acceptance test or outcome. If a metric cannot point to a decision, delete it before a colleague does. Synthetic baselines are allowed for the portfolio; label them synthetic so you never confuse them with production truth in a conversation. Put the six rows where engineering and risk can both edit them.

example.title: False-positive rate with a formula
example.story: Metric: false-positive rate. Formula: FP / (FP+TP) over 7 days, where TP means an alert followed by a documented risk-reducing action within 24 hours, and FP means closed as 'no action / known inventory' without a risk change. Source: alert table joined to case dispositions. Baseline: 79% FP on synthetic week-4 counts (95 FP of 120). 90-day target: ≤40% FP without raising missed incidents. This is computable only if disposition codes exist; if not, mark blocked and name field disposition_code.
example.takeaway: A metric without a disposition definition will be gamed or abandoned.

lessons.title: The six-row dictionary
body: Incident rate: count of true risk events per 100 accounts per week — define true the same way as in acceptance tests. Detection coverage: true events that had a prior alert divided by all true events. Manual minutes per case: median analyst time from alert to disposition. Loss exposure: dollars in accounts that breached the control’s intent, whether or not alerted. Decision latency: median minutes from alert to first human acknowledgement. False-positive rate completes the six.

For each row write source systems in plain English — alert store, case tool, positions marks. No vendor secrets required; synthetic warehouses are fine for the portfolio. State the join keys you need (account_id, alert_id, ts). Missing join keys are how coverage metrics die quietly after launch when nobody can rebuild the number.

Targets should be numeric and dated. Improve latency fails the dictionary; median ack under 10 minutes by day 90 passes. Put the six rows in one table so a colleague can delete one with a pen. That delete exercise is the industry task this week — design the table to make the argument easy. Star the two metrics you will watch in the first 48 hours after any parameter ship.

example.title: Decision latency row
example.story: Metric: decision latency. Formula: median(ack_timestamp − alert_timestamp) for CONC_5 alerts, excluding snoozed-during-maintenance windows. Source: alert store + ack events. Baseline: 27 minutes on a 14-day shadow. 90-day target: 10 minutes. Computable now if ack events exist; if officers ack in chat instead of the tool, blocked on missing ack_timestamp — the fix is a one-click ack, not a better chart.
example.takeaway: If the action happens outside the tool, your latency metric is fiction until you capture the ack.

lessons.title: Computable versus blocked
body: Mark two metrics computable from data you already have — or can synthesize honestly for the exercise — and two that are blocked. For each blocked metric, name the missing field. This is the conversation that unlocks engineering time: you are not asking for better analytics; you are asking for disposition_code or adjEq in the payload. Field names beat adjectives every time in a planning meeting.

Take the dictionary to a risk colleague and ask them to delete one metric. Record which and why. Scarcity forces prioritization; six rows that everyone loves usually means nobody is choosing. Log the deletion even if you disagree. You can restore a metric in phase two with the missing field still named so it does not become a vague backlog wish.

Carry the surviving metrics into week 8’s pass rule and week 11’s 48-hour watch list. If false-positive rate is your launch metric, the replay pass rule should not optimize a different vanity count. Consistency across weeks is part of looking like someone who owns a slice rather than a sequence of homework. Bring missing-field names as ticket titles to the next engineering sync.

example.title: Colleague deletes loss exposure
example.story: Dictionary shown to a colleague. They delete loss exposure for the first 90 days: 'We cannot attribute preventable loss without a clean counterfactual; it will turn into storytelling.' They keep false-positive rate and decision latency as the launch pair. You log the deletion reason and demote loss exposure to a phase-2 metric with missing field counterfactual_loss_usd still named.
example.takeaway: A deleted metric with a reason is healthier than a zombie metric on a dashboard.

lab.goal: Fill the six-row metric dictionary and label two computable and two blocked metrics with missing fields.

steps: Create a table with columns: name, formula, source, baseline, 90-day target, status (computable/blocked), missing field if blocked.

weeks.title: Parameter dictionary and maker-checker

sessions.text: Read one public OKX position-tier change notice from start to finish (okx.com help center). Map it onto proposer, approver, effective time, and rollback. This is the public pattern for parameter governance, not a template to copy onto an employer system.

Parameter dictionary with 8 rows: threshold, haircut, tier bound, stale-price window, max leverage, concentration cap, alert cooldown, maker-checker limit. Columns: name, unit, owner, who may change it, simulation required, backtest required, what is monitored after the change.
Write the approval workflow in six steps. Step one must state who is forbidden from approving their own change.
Ask one risk or product person how their firm separates the person who proposes a parameter change from the person who approves it. Write their answer in five lines.

criteria: Eight parameters are documented with owner, change right, and whether simulation and backtest are required.
The six-step workflow blocks self-approval in writing.
One practitioner’s answer on proposer versus approver is saved.
weeks.goal: Document eight risk parameters with owners and change rights, and write a six-step maker-checker workflow that forbids self-approval.
weeks.bigIdea: Parameters are product surface area: thresholds, haircuts, tier bounds, cooldowns. Maker-checker means the person who proposes a change cannot be the same person who approves it. Public exchange notices about position-tier changes are a readable pattern for proposer, approver, effective time, and rollback — use them as study material, not as a template to copy onto an employer system. If a parameter can move money or silence alerts, it belongs in a dictionary with simulation and backtest flags.

lessons.title: Read a public parameter change as governance
body: Find one public OKX (or similar) position-tier change notice and read it end to end. Map four fields: who effectively proposes, who approves, effective time, and rollback or contact path. Approver is often invisible in public notices — note that gap explicitly. Your learning target is the shape of the announcement, not their commercial motives. Do not copy the notice into an employer system as a template for production process.

Translate to an internal design you might own later: proposer role, approver role, effective timestamp, rollback parameter set. Write the forbidden case clearly in your notes: proposer equals approver. Synthetic roles are enough for the portfolio: Trading Risk Proposer, Risk Platform Approver, On-call Publisher. The point is separation of duties you can implement, not org-chart cosplay with real names.

Every parameter change needs a monitored post-change metric for the first 48 hours — alert volume, liquidation count, or false-positive rate from week 6. If the public notice omits rollback, your design must not omit it. Week 8 will replay a change; week 11 will ship with rollback as a config action. This week installs the governance spine those weeks hang on.

example.title: Mapping a public tier notice
example.story: A public notice says MMR for BTCUSDT tier 3 rises from 1.0% to 1.5% effective 2026-04-01 08:00 UTC. Your map: proposer = risk policy team (inferred); approver = not disclosed publicly; effective time = that UTC stamp; rollback = not stated, so you mark rollback as 'unpublished — design must not omit this'. Lesson for your dictionary: every row needs a monitored post-change metric, e.g. liquidation count and alert volume for 48 hours.
example.takeaway: If rollback is invisible in the public pattern, make it explicit in yours.

lessons.title: Eight-row parameter dictionary
body: Rows required: threshold; haircut; tier bound; stale-price window; max leverage; concentration cap; alert cooldown; maker-checker limit (the maximum change a single approval may pass, or the dual-control size trigger). Columns: name; unit; owner; who may change it; simulation required (yes/no); backtest required (yes/no); what is monitored after the change. Fill every cell; blanks become skipped work under deadline pressure and quiet production risk.

Be concrete on units: percent of adjEq, basis points, seconds, dollars of notional. Vague units produce vague approvals. Simulation means a forward-looking or scenario check; backtest or replay means historical accounts under the new parameter. Week 8 will execute a replay — set those flags now so week 8 is scheduled work, not a surprise you discover the night before ship.

Owner and who may change it should be roles, not named individuals who leave. Maker-checker limit can be a size trigger: changes of 1.0 percentage point or more need a second approver; smaller changes still need a different human than the proposer. Write that rule into the dictionary row, not only into tribal knowledge. Review the dictionary quarterly; freeze parameters with no owner.

example.title: Concentration cap row
example.story: Name: concentration_cap. Unit: percent of adjEq. Owner: Trading Risk Manager. Who may change: Risk Proposer role via change request. Simulation required: yes (stress names +20% jump). Backtest required: yes (20-account replay minimum). Monitor after: alert count, false-positive rate, max single-name loss for 48 hours. Maker-checker: changes ≥1.0 percentage point need a second approver; sub-1.0 still need a different human than the proposer.
example.takeaway: Flags for simulation and backtest should be boring and always filled — blank means someone will skip the work.

lessons.title: Six-step approval workflow
body: Write six steps. Step one must state who is forbidden from approving their own change. Later steps cover validation, simulation or replay evidence, approval, publish, and monitor or rollback. Keep it implementable: each step has an artifact such as ticket id, replay notebook hash, approval record, or config version. Culture is not a control; artifacts are what auditors and on-call can find at 2 a.m.

Self-approval must be impossible in the workflow text. Phrases like should not approve their own change fail the test. Prefer system blocks proposer user id from the approver field. If you only have a paper process for the portfolio, write the block as a required checklist item with two signatures from different people and different roles, and store the signed page with the change id.

Industry ask this week: how a real firm separates proposer and approver. Capture five lines. Compare to your six steps without copying confidential process diagrams. Note one difference you might adopt and one you will not, with a one-line reason for each choice. Time-box step 6: if the 48-hour monitors are not named, publish is incomplete.

example.title: Six steps with self-approval blocked
example.story: (1) Proposer opens change request; system blocks proposer user id from the approver field. (2) Schema and unit validation run automatically. (3) If dictionary says simulation required, attach scenario result; if backtest required, attach replay with seed and pass rule. (4) Approver (different human, listed role) signs. (5) Publisher pushes config with effective time and prior version pointer for rollback. (6) On-call watches the two monitor metrics for 48 hours and reverts on breach. Artifact ids recorded at each step.
example.takeaway: Self-approval must be impossible in the workflow text, not merely discouraged in culture.

weeks.title: Replay the change before it ships

sessions.text: Define, in your own words, historical replay, stress, and production shadow. Reread stress_testing.py in this repo and list what it does not do: no Greeks, no collateral-haircut path, no partial liquidation.

Specify one parameter change: raise a concentration cap from X to Y, using synthetic X and Y. Define population, window, metric, and a numeric pass rule. The pass rule must be a number, not the word acceptable.
Run the replay on 20 synthetic accounts. Print alert counts before and after the change. Keep the seed in the notebook so you can rerun it.
Send only the pass rule, not the data, to one person. Ask whether it is too tight. Log the answer.

criteria: The pass rule is a single number with a unit.
The notebook prints before and after alert counts on 20 synthetic accounts and shows the random seed.
One review of the pass rule is logged.
weeks.goal: Specify one parameter change with a numeric pass rule, replay it on 20 synthetic accounts with a fixed seed, and print alert counts before and after.
weeks.bigIdea: Historical replay runs a new rule over past accounts and marks; stress pushes scenario shocks; production shadow runs the new rule in parallel without enforcing it. They are not interchangeable. A pass rule must be a number with a unit ('alerts increase by at most 5 on the 20-account set'), not the word acceptable. If you cannot rerun the notebook from a seed and get the same before/after counts, you do not yet have evidence — you have a vibe.

lessons.title: Replay versus stress versus shadow
body: Historical replay: freeze a population and window; compute the metric under old and new parameters. Stress: apply hypothetical shocks such as spot down 20 percent or vol doubled whether or not they occurred. Production shadow: emit candidate alerts beside production without acting. Your study task includes rereading stress_testing.py in this repo and listing what it does not do: no Greeks, no collateral-haircut path, no partial liquidation. That honesty belongs in the spec.

Choose one change: raise a concentration cap from X to Y with synthetic X and Y. Define population (20 accounts), window (for example 30 synthetic days), metric (alert count), and a numeric pass rule. Link back to week 7: this change should already have simulation and backtest flags set to yes. If the dictionary said backtest required, this lab is that backtest and should look like evidence, not a sketch.

Write the pass rule before you look at the after counts. Changing the rule after seeing the number is how silent regressions get a green stamp. If the first run fails, either fix the change or accept FAIL and redesign — do not quietly widen acceptable. Send only the pass rule to a reviewer this week; their job is to judge tightness, not to re-litigate your synthetic accounts.

example.title: Numeric pass rule
example.story: Change: concentration_cap from 5.0% to 6.0% of adjEq. Population: 20 synthetic accounts. Window: 30 days of marks. Metric: number of CONC alerts under the cap rule. Pass rule: after-count − before-count ≤ 5 alerts total on the set, and no account with a synthetic 'true incident' flag loses coverage (incidents still alerted under the new cap). If after-count is 18 and before-count is 11, delta = 7 → fail. If after is 14 and before is 11, delta = 3 → pass pending incident-coverage check.
example.takeaway: If the pass rule cannot fail on a printed number, it is not a pass rule.

lessons.title: Synthetic replay you can rerun
body: Build 20 accounts with a fixed random seed. Each account needs adjEq, top-name notional or a concentration ratio, and optionally a true-incident flag. Compute alerts when concentration exceeds the cap for old and new caps. Print counts before and after. Keep the seed in the notebook so a second run matches bit for bit. Always print seed, before, after, and delta — never only a chart that cannot be audited.

Do not chase realism theater. Diversify a few accounts near the band so the cap change actually moves the count; if every account is at 1 percent or 20 percent, your replay is idle and will pass for the wrong reason. Aim for several accounts between 5 percent and 6 percent if those are your X and Y so the delta is informative.

Record an inputs hash habit: seed, cap_before, cap_after, n_accounts. That habit returns in week 9’s event schema as inputs_hash. Evaluate PASS or FAIL from the stated rule in the same cell that prints the counts. List beside the results the three gaps in stress_testing.py so readers know what this evidence does not cover. Put the seed in the write-up too.

example.title: Before/after on 20 accounts
example.story: Seed 42. Cap before 5%, after 6%. Suppose 11 accounts alert at 5% and 8 alert at 6% because three accounts sat between 5% and 6%. Printed line: seed=42 before=11 after=8 delta=-3. Pass rule was delta ≤ +5 and no lost incidents; if those three were false positives, you pass. If one of the three had true_incident=1, you fail despite fewer alerts — coverage matters.
example.takeaway: Always print seed, before, after, delta; never only a chart.

lab.goal: Run a replay on 20 synthetic accounts, print alert counts before and after a concentration-cap change, and keep a fixed seed.
lab.why: Shipping without a rerunnable before/after count is how silent risk regressions enter production.
steps: In a notebook, set seed = 42 (or another fixed integer you document) via numpy.random.default_rng(seed).
Generate 20 accounts: adjEq uniform between 50_000 and 2_000_000; concentration_ratio uniform between 0.02 and 0.12; optional true_incident = 1 when ratio > 0.10.
Choose cap_before = 0.05 and cap_after = 0.06 (or your X/Y).
Alert if concentration_ratio > cap. Count before and after. Print seed, before, after, delta.
Evaluate your numeric pass rule; print PASS or FAIL.
List three things stress_testing.py does not do (no Greeks, no haircut path, no partial liquidation) beside the results.
expected: Printed seed and before/after alert counts on 20 accounts.
A numeric pass rule evaluated to PASS or FAIL.
Note on replay vs stress vs shadow in your own words.

weeks.title: Events, APIs, and the path from tick to alert

sessions.text: Design a limit as a REST resource: GET and POST, and what makes a POST idempotent. Then read Martin Fowler, What do you mean by Event-Driven? (martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html). You are learning the vocabulary, not standing up Kafka.
One-page box-and-arrow diagram: market tick, position, metric, rule, alert, human acknowledgement. Mark each arrow sync or async. Name the system of record at each box.
Write JSON examples, not just schemas, for AlertEvent and for a parameter-change command. Both include a correlation id and an inputs hash.
Ask one engineer which arrow on your diagram is actually a queue today. Write down the answer, including I do not know.

criteria: Diagram marks every arrow sync or async and names a system of record.
Both JSON examples contain a correlation id and an inputs hash, and a second example you type by hand still matches the fields.
One engineer’s answer about the queue is logged.
weeks.goal: Draw the tick-to-alert path with sync/async arrows and systems of record, and write JSON examples for AlertEvent and a parameter-change command with correlation id and inputs hash.
weeks.bigIdea: A limit should be designed as a resource you can GET and POST, with POST idempotency so retries do not create duplicate limits. Event-driven architecture means components communicate by emitting facts ('mark updated', 'alert raised') rather than only by synchronous request/response — learn the vocabulary from Martin Fowler’s event-driven article without standing up Kafka. The path from market tick to human acknowledgement is a chain of stores and arrows; each arrow is sync or async, and each box has a system of record. Correlation ids and inputs hashes make replay and RCA possible.

lessons.title: Limits as REST resources with idempotent POST
body: Treat a risk limit as a resource: GET /limits/{id} returns the current parameter set; POST /limits or POST /limit-changes submits a change. Idempotency means doing the same POST twice has the same effect as once. Practical pattern: client sends an Idempotency-Key header or a change_id; the server stores the result of the first accepted request and returns it again on retries. You are specifying behavior, not deploying an API gateway this week.

Without idempotency, a flaky network plus a retried approve call can publish twice or fork versions. That is a risk incident waiting for a busy day. Write the happy path and the retry path in a few lines each. Include the conflict case: same change_id with a different body returns 409 Conflict rather than silently overwriting a published version.

Connect this to week 7’s maker-checker: the POST body should carry proposer, approver, and change_id, and the server should reject proposer equals approver before publish. Idempotency and maker-checker solve different failures — duplicates versus self-dealing — and both belong on the parameter-change path before week 11’s release plan. Add the idempotency contract to that checklist.

example.title: Idempotent parameter change POST
example.story: Client posts change_id=chg_7f3a to raise concentration_cap to 6.0 with inputs_hash=sha256:ab… and correlation_id=corr_221. Server accepts, creates version 14, returns 201. Client times out, posts the same change_id again. Server returns 200 with version 14 and does not create version 15. A different body with the same change_id returns 409 Conflict. That contract is what on-call needs when the publisher retries.
example.takeaway: Idempotency keys turn 'maybe it published' into a deterministic read.

lessons.title: Tick → position → metric → rule → alert → ack
body: Draw one page with six boxes: market tick, position, metric, rule, alert, human acknowledgement. Mark each arrow sync or async. Name the system of record at each box — mark feed, position store, metric cache, rule config, alert store, case tool. Unlabeled arrows become production mysteries; label them while the page is still simple enough to redraw in a meeting without a tool fight.

A typical pattern: ticks arrive async into marks; position service may be sync on query; metric calculation may be async stream or micro-batch; rule evaluation async; alert write async; human ack sync into the case tool. Your diagram can differ. What matters is that every arrow is labeled and every box has a home. Note calc lag as a risk on the metric arrow even though paging thresholds are week 10’s job.

Read Fowler’s What do you mean by Event-Driven? for vocabulary only — event notification, event-carried state transfer, and related terms — not as a license to propose a new bus. Ask an engineer which arrow is actually a queue today. Log I do not know if that is the answer; honesty beats invented topic names in a portfolio note that someone else will read later.

example.title: Labeled path fragment
example.story: Tick (mark feed SoR) --async--> Mark service; Mark+Position (position SoR) --async--> Metric worker computes concentration_ratio; Metric --sync on read--> Rule engine with config SoR parameter store; Rule --async--> Alert store; Alert --async notify--> Officer; Officer --sync--> Ack in case tool. Failure mode: if metric worker lags 90 seconds, alerts describe a past world — page on calc lag belongs in week 10, but note it now on the diagram as a risk.
example.takeaway: Unlabeled arrows become production mysteries; label sync/async while the page is still simple.

lessons.title: JSON you can hash and correlate
body: Write example JSON, not only schemas, for AlertEvent and for a parameter-change command. Both include correlation_id and inputs_hash. Correlation_id ties tick to metric to alert to ack across services. Inputs_hash fingerprints the inputs that justified the decision so RCA can see whether marks or parameters drifted. Keep payloads free of employer secrets; use synthetic account ids only in every example.

Type a second AlertEvent example by hand that still matches the field set — that is your check that the shape is usable, not only pretty. If the second example needs new keys to make sense, the schema is wrong. Prefer stable keys: type, alert_code, account_id, metric_value, threshold, correlation_id, inputs_hash, ts. Resist optional keys that only one producer understands.

Reuse week 8’s habit: the replay notebook’s seed and caps belong in an inputs_hash for the parameter-change command. The alert’s inputs_hash should cover account marks and the threshold version used. When those hashes disagree with what on-call expects, you have a lead; when they are absent, you have timestamps and luck. Store one golden pair of examples next to the diagram.

example.title: AlertEvent and change command
example.story: AlertEvent: {"type":"AlertEvent","alert_code":"CONC_5","account_id":"syn_014","metric_value":0.062,"threshold":0.05,"correlation_id":"corr_221","inputs_hash":"sha256:4b1c…","ts":"2026-04-02T12:01:03Z"}. Parameter-change command: {"type":"ParameterChangeCommand","parameter":"concentration_cap","from":0.05,"to":0.06,"change_id":"chg_7f3a","proposer":"user_a","approver":"user_b","correlation_id":"corr_900","inputs_hash":"sha256:9de0…","effective_ts":"2026-04-03T08:00:00Z"}. A second hand-typed AlertEvent for account syn_015 must reuse the same keys even if values differ.
example.takeaway: If you cannot point to correlation_id in both alert and change, cross-system RCA will rely on timestamps and luck.
