weeks.title: System of record and five pages worth sending

sessions.text: Write the difference between the store that serves today’s decision and the store that replays last quarter. Then apply three operational signals to a risk calculation: lag, error rate, and saturation. A textbook chapter is optional. Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Ch. 1 and the replication overview in Ch. 5 are enough if you already own the book.
Storage note with four domains: positions, marks, parameters, decisions. For each: system of record, who may write, and how long an RCA pack must keep it.
Five pages an on-call would wake up for: calc lag, missing marks, rule-engine errors, queue depth, parameter-publish failure. Each needs a numeric threshold and an owner.
One message or conversation: how does an incident get detected before a trader complains? Log the answer in five lines.

criteria: Four domains each have a system of record, a writer, and a retention statement.
Five paging alerts each have a number and an owner.
One detection-before-complaint note is saved.
weeks.goal: Name the system of record for positions, marks, parameters, and decisions, and define five paging alerts an on-call would wake for.
weeks.bigIdea: A risk platform is only as trustworthy as the store that owns each fact. System of record means the one place you treat as authoritative for a domain when two systems disagree. Operational signals—lag (how late the calc is), error rate (how often it fails), and saturation (how full the queues or CPUs are)—tell you the platform is sick before a trader complains. Five well-owned paging alerts beat fifty dashboards nobody watches.

lessons.title: System of record versus replay store
body: System of record means the authoritative store for a fact when systems disagree. For today's trading decision you need the live position and mark that the risk engine is using right now. For last quarter's root-cause analysis (RCA) you need a replay store that keeps what the engine saw then, not a corrected backfill. Confusing the two is how teams 'fix' history and lose the audit trail.

Apply three operational signals to any risk calculation. Lag is the age of the last successful result versus wall-clock time; if VaR for the Asia book is twenty minutes late at the open, the desk is flying blind. Error rate is failed runs over attempted runs in a window; a spike often means a schema break or a bad mark feed. Saturation is how close a queue, CPU, or database connection pool sits to its limit; when saturation stays high, lag and errors follow. You do not need a textbook to use these words in a design review—you need to say which metric you would page on.

Write the difference in one sentence you can defend: the decision store answers 'what do we believe now,' and the replay store answers 'what did we believe then.' Retention for RCA packs is usually longer than retention for hot caches. If your firm already owns Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications, chapters 1 and the replication overview in chapter 5 are enough background; the deliverable this week is the ownership map, not a distributed-systems essay.

example.title: Two stores, one wrong mark
example.story: At 09:05 the risk UI shows BTC mark 98,200 from the cache, while the pricing library just wrote 97,800 to the mark service. A limit check uses the cache and understates delta by about 0.4%. The RCA pack three weeks later must replay against the mark service snapshot at 09:05 (97,800), not today's corrected history. If you only kept the cache, you cannot explain why the alert did not fire.
example.takeaway: Decide which store owns the truth for the decision, and which snapshot owns the truth for the investigation.

lessons.title: Four domains: positions, marks, parameters, decisions
body: Map four domains and refuse to leave any blank. Positions: who writes fills and bookings, and which system is authoritative after a cancel-replace. Marks: who publishes the price used in risk, and what happens when the feed is stale. Parameters: thresholds, haircuts, and tiers—often changed by risk product with maker-checker, not by the overnight batch alone. Decisions: alert outcomes, overrides, and acknowledgements; these are operational facts that auditors will ask for.

For each domain write three fields: system of record (name a real or plausible system, for example Murex for books and positions, a market-data service for marks, a parameter service for limits, an alert store for decisions), who may write (role, not a person's name), and how long an RCA pack must keep it (for example 90 days hot plus seven years archive, or whatever your study plan assumes—pick a number and state it). Writer rights matter: if anyone can PATCH a threshold in production without an approval id, your week-7 maker-checker work was theater.

Keep the note short enough that an on-call can open it at 2 a.m. Prefer tables over prose. If two systems claim the same domain, pick one as system of record and label the other as a projection or cache. That single sentence prevents half of the 'which number is right' arguments you will hear in trading risk.

example.title: Parameter domain row
example.story: Domain: parameters. System of record: risk-parameter service (versioned JSON). Who may write: Risk Product proposes; Market Risk Control approves; CI applies. RCA retention: every published version for 2 years, including the version id embedded in each alert. A change from concentration cap 15% to 18% is stored as version 1042 with proposer id, approver id, and effective timestamp 2026-03-12T14:00:00Z.
example.takeaway: If the alert does not carry the parameter version, the RCA pack cannot prove which rule fired.

lessons.title: Five pages worth sending
body: Paging alert means an alert that pages a human because the platform itself is unsafe, not because a desk breached a trading limit. Limit breaches go to the desk workflow; platform pages go to on-call. Define five: calculation lag, missing marks, rule-engine errors, queue depth, and parameter-publish failure. Each needs a numeric threshold and a named owner role.

Draft thresholds you can defend with arithmetic. Example shapes: calc lag pages if the last successful book-level VaR is older than 10 minutes during the trading window. Missing marks pages if more than 2% of in-scope underlyings have mark age over 5 minutes. Rule-engine errors page if the 5-minute error rate exceeds 1%. Queue depth pages if the alert or market-data consumer lag exceeds 50,000 messages or 3 minutes of consumer lag. Parameter-publish failure pages on any failed promote to production or any publish that does not receive an acknowledgement within 60 seconds.

Owners must be roles that can act: Risk Platform On-call for lag and queues, Market Data On-call for marks, Risk Engine On-call for rule errors, Risk Product On-call for parameter publish. Write the page text template in one line each so the pager is not a mystery novel. This week you are not implementing Prometheus; you are writing the contract that would make an implementer stop guessing.

example.title: Calc-lag page that is specific enough
example.story: Alert name: risk_calc_lag_high. Condition: max(now - last_success_ts) across books in {EQ_ASIA, EQ_EU} > 600 seconds while session_open = true. Severity: page. Owner: Risk Platform On-call. Runbook first step: check the last job id in the calc orchestrator; if the job is stuck, fail over to the standby worker pool; if marks are the blocker, page Market Data. Without the 600-second number, overnight noise and true incidents look the same.
example.takeaway: A page without a number and an owner is a dashboard widget, not an operational control.

lab.goal: Produce a storage note for four domains and a five-row paging-alert table with thresholds and owners.
lab.why: Platform reliability for Trading Risk starts with ownership and wake-up criteria, not with another chart.
steps: Create a markdown or CSV file named week10_storage_and_pages.md in your study folder.

Add a table with columns: domain, system_of_record, who_may_write, rca_retention. Rows: positions, marks, parameters, decisions. Fill every cell; invent plausible system names if you lack employer detail, and label them synthetic.

Add a second table with columns: alert_name, condition_with_number, unit, owner_role, first_runbook_step. Rows must be exactly: calc_lag, missing_marks, rule_engine_errors, queue_depth, parameter_publish_failure.

For calc_lag use a threshold in seconds (for example 600). For missing_marks use a percent of underlyings (for example 2). For rule_engine_errors use a percent in a 5-minute window (for example 1). For queue_depth use message count or consumer-lag minutes. For parameter_publish_failure use a timeout in seconds (for example 60) or 'any failed promote'.

Write five lines titled 'decision vs replay': one sentence on what the decision store answers, one on what the replay store answers, and three sentences mapping lag, error rate, and saturation to your five pages.
Self-check: every domain row has all three ownership fields; every alert row has a number and an owner role.
expected: Four domain rows with system of record, writer role, and retention.
Five paging alerts each with a numeric threshold (or explicit any-fail) and an owner role.
A short note that separates decision store from replay store and ties lag, error rate, and saturation to pages.

weeks.title: Ship a risk change with a rollback

sessions.text: Write a minimal delivery path: test, review, staged config, rollback. Do not take a Kubernetes course. The test of understanding is whether rollback is a config action.
Release plan for the week-8 parameter change. Include the tests that must pass, who signs UAT, the shadow period, the rollback action, and the two numbers you watch for 48 hours.
Name three automated checks: schema valid, no self-approval, replay still meets the week-8 pass rule. Describe each check as an input and a pass/fail output.
Ask someone who has shipped a risk change what they wish had been monitored in the first day. Log it.

criteria: Release plan contains a rollback that is a config or parameter revert, and two numbers watched for 48 hours.
Three checks are specified as input plus pass/fail output.
One production monitoring lesson is logged.
weeks.goal: Ship the week-8 parameter change with tests, UAT, shadow, rollback as a config action, and two numbers watched for 48 hours.
weeks.bigIdea: A risk change is not 'deployed' when the code merges; it is shipped when you can undo it without a heroics weekend. Rollback should be a configuration or parameter revert to a known version, not a git archaeology session. Automated checks—schema valid, no self-approval, replay still meets the pass rule—turn governance into something a pipeline can enforce. The first 48 hours after promote are part of the change, not an afterthought.

lessons.title: Minimal delivery path: test, review, stage, rollback
body: Write a delivery path that a Trading Risk parameter change can actually follow. Test means the replay and unit checks from week 8 still pass on the candidate value. Review means a second human who is not the proposer signs UAT (user acceptance testing: a named person confirms the change is fit for the stated use). Staged config means the new parameter version is published to a shadow or canary scope before firm-wide promote. Rollback means pointing production at the previous parameter version id in one action.

You do not need a Kubernetes course to understand this. Containers and clusters are irrelevant if the business object is a versioned threshold. The test of understanding is whether rollback is a config action: 'set concentration_cap to version 1041' rather than 'rebuild the image from last Tuesday.' If rollback requires a developer to be awake, you have a staffing dependency, not a control.

Keep the path on one page. Boxes: propose → automated checks → UAT sign-off → shadow period → promote → 48-hour watch → optional rollback. Every arrow should name an artifact (test report, approval id, version id). This is the same maker-checker idea as week 7, now attached to release mechanics.

example.title: Rollback that is one field
example.story: Week-8 change: raise concentration_cap from 15% to 18% as parameter version 1042. Shadow for 24 hours on synthetic book desk_sim_A. Promote at Tuesday 16:00 UTC. At Wednesday 10:00, alert count for concentration breaches jumps from 3/day to 40/day against the week-8 pass rule of 'post-change daily alerts ≤ 12 on the 20-account replay population.' Rollback action: publish version 1041 (15%) with reason code ROLLBACK_ALERT_SPIKE. No code deploy.
example.takeaway: If you cannot name the previous version id, you do not have a rollback.

lessons.title: Release plan for the week-8 change
body: Build a release plan that references your week-8 parameter change by name. Include: the tests that must pass (replay on 20 synthetic accounts, seed recorded, pass rule met), who signs UAT (role and what they look at), the shadow period (duration and scope), the rollback action (version revert), and the two numbers you watch for 48 hours after promote. User acceptance testing (UAT) means a named human confirms the change is fit for the stated use before firm-wide promote.

Choose two watch numbers that detect harm early. Good pair: (1) daily concentration-alert count on the in-scope population, (2) percent of accounts with utilization above 90% of the new cap. Bad pair: vanity metrics that cannot move in 48 hours. State baseline from the week-8 before numbers and the tripwire that triggers rollback discussion. If a watch metric needs a data field you do not have, rename the metric—do not invent a dashboard you cannot compute.

UAT is not a rubber stamp. The signer should see the before/after alert counts, the pass rule, and the rollback command. Write the sign-off line as a sentence the signer would actually type: 'I approve version 1042 for promote; rollback is revert to 1041; I reviewed replay seed 42 with alerts 8 → 5 against pass rule ≤ 12.' That sentence becomes the audit artifact when someone asks who let the change through.

example.title: Two numbers for 48 hours
example.story: Watch A: concentration alerts per day on the 20-account synthetic cohort, baseline 8, rollback review if any rolling 24h count > 12. Watch B: share of those accounts with concentration > 90% of cap, baseline 10% (2 of 20), rollback review if share > 25% for 6 hours. Both are computable from the same alert and position feeds you already assumed in week 8.
example.takeaway: Pick watch metrics you can plot the same day, not quarterly KRIs.

lessons.title: Three automated checks as input and pass/fail
body: Name three automated checks and describe each as an input plus a pass/fail output. Check 1: schema valid—input is the parameter JSON against the published schema; output PASS if required fields and types match, else FAIL with the failing path. Check 2: no self-approval—input is proposer id and approver id; output FAIL if they are equal or if either is missing. Check 3: replay still meets the week-8 pass rule—input is candidate parameter value, seed, and account set; output PASS if the metric meets the numeric rule, else FAIL with before/after counts.

These checks belong in the pipeline before promote, not in a wiki. Writing them as input/output contracts lets an engineer implement them without debating philosophy. If your environment cannot run a real pipeline, still write the contract; the study plan grades the specification. Each FAIL should block promote and notify a role: Risk Product On-call for schema and self-approval failures, Model or Risk Analytics On-call for replay failures.

Do not expand into a full DevOps platform. Three checks that gate one parameter change teach more than a half-finished CI diagram. Tie each FAIL to a human message: who is told, that promote is blocked, and which artifact to open next (schema diff, approval record, or replay notebook). That is enough to claim you can ship a risk change with rollback discipline.

example.title: Self-approval check
example.story: Input: {"proposer": "alex.risk", "approver": "alex.risk", "version": 1042}. Output: FAIL reason=SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN. Input with approver "sam.control" → PASS. The release plan states that a FAIL stops the staged publish job and notifies Risk Product On-call.
example.takeaway: Governance that is not a pass/fail gate will be skipped under time pressure.

weeks.title: Historical and parametric VaR, computed

sessions.text: Hull 11th ed. Ch. 22 on historical simulation and the model-building (variance-covariance) approach. Do the arithmetic. Skip any section you can already recite from FRM without a calculation.

Seed numpy Generator with 7. Draw 250 days by 2 standard normals. Apply correlation 0.4, daily vols 1% and 2%, weights 60/40, book value 1,000,000. Report 99% 1-day historical VaR using NumPy’s default quantile, and parametric VaR using 2.326 as the normal factor.
Eight lines: on which days these two VaR numbers diverge, and which one you would not show a treasurer without a footnote.
If a week-4 conversation is due a follow-up, send it. If not, read one public market-risk note and file five lines plus the URL.

criteria: Historical 99% VaR prints between 29,300 and 29,450. Parametric 99% VaR prints between 27,300 and 27,450. Seed 7 is in the notebook.
The eight-line note names a case where the two methods diverge.
Either a follow-up was sent, or a public note is filed with a URL.
weeks.goal: Compute 99% one-day historical and parametric VaR on a seeded two-asset book and know when the two numbers diverge.
weeks.bigIdea: Value at Risk (VaR) is a loss threshold: with a stated probability, losses over a horizon should not exceed that number under the model's assumptions. Historical VaR reads the empirical loss distribution from past (or simulated) P&L. Parametric VaR assumes a normal portfolio return and scales volatility by a z-factor. Same book, same day count, different assumptions—so the numbers will not match, and a treasurer deserves a footnote when you pick one.

lessons.title: Historical simulation VaR in plain English
body: Historical VaR lines up past portfolio P&L (or P&L rebuilt from returns), sorts the loss side, and reads a quantile. For 99% one-day VaR you look near the worst 1% of days. If VaR is reported as a positive loss number, you take the 99% quantile of losses, where loss is minus P&L. NumPy's default quantile (linear interpolation) is what this lab uses so everyone lands in the same band.

In this week's lab you do not download market history. You simulate 250 days of returns for two assets so the exercise is reproducible. Seed the NumPy Generator with 7. Draw a 250 by 2 matrix of standard normals. Impose correlation 0.4 with a Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix, scale columns by daily volatilities 1% and 2%, apply weights 60% and 40%, and multiply portfolio returns by book value 1,000,000 to get P&L. Historical 99% VaR on that loss series should print between about 29,300 and 29,450.

Jargon in one line: quantile means the cut point where a stated fraction of observations lie below it. Cholesky factor means a lower-triangular matrix L such that L L-transpose equals the correlation matrix, used to turn independent normals into correlated normals. Keep the seed in the notebook; without it the lab is not a lab.

example.title: Reading the 99% historical VaR
example.story: After building 250 portfolio P&L values with seed 7, define loss = -P&L. Sort losses ascending. The default NumPy 0.99 quantile interpolates near the third-worst losses and yields roughly 29,370 (accept 29,300–29,450). That means: under this simulated history, only about 1% of days lose more than ~29.4k on the 1,000,000 book.
example.takeaway: Historical VaR is only as honest as the return sample you fed it—including a synthetic sample you must label as synthetic.

lessons.title: Parametric (variance-covariance) VaR
body: Parametric VaR, also called the model-building or variance-covariance approach, assumes portfolio returns are normal. You compute portfolio standard deviation from asset vols, weights, and correlations, then multiply by a normal z-factor and by book value. For 99% one-sided, z = 2.326 is the usual factor (the 99th percentile of the standard normal).

Plain English formula: portfolio variance equals w-transpose times Sigma times w, where Sigma is the covariance matrix. With daily vols σ1=0.01, σ2=0.02, correlation ρ=0.4, and weights 0.6 and 0.4, each covariance entry is ρ_ij × σ_i × σ_j. Portfolio vol σ_p is the square root of that variance. Parametric 99% VaR ≈ 2.326 × σ_p × 1,000,000, which lands between about 27,300 and 27,450 (around 27,364 with these inputs). No path simulation is required once Sigma and weights are set.

Why is parametric lower than historical here? The normal assumption underweights fat tails that appear in your finite simulated sample. That is not a bug in your code; it is the method talking. Hull's chapter on historical simulation versus the model-building approach is the study backbone—do the arithmetic, do not only memorize names.

example.title: Portfolio vol then parametric VaR
example.story: Sigma_11=0.01², Sigma_22=0.02², Sigma_12=Sigma_21=0.4×0.01×0.02. With w=[0.6,0.4], σ_p ≈ 0.011764. Then 2.326 × 0.011764 × 1,000,000 ≈ 27,364. Same book as the historical lab; different assumption about the shape of the loss distribution.
example.takeaway: Parametric VaR is a closed-form scaling of volatility; it cannot 'see' a weird day in the sample unless that day changes Sigma.

lessons.title: When the two VaRs diverge—and what you show a treasurer
body: The two numbers diverge when the empirical loss distribution is not normal: skew, fat tails, or a few dominant crash days. They also diverge when you refresh historical windows but leave Sigma stale, or when options and other non-linear products make delta-normal covariance a cartoon. In linear two-asset equity-like books the gap is often modest; in crisis windows it is the whole story. On this seeded lab book the gap is about two thousand dollars—historical near 29.4k, parametric near 27.4k.

Write eight lines that name a concrete case. Example shape: 'On days when both assets gap down together beyond 2.5 σ, historical VaR rises with those days in the window; parametric VaR only moves if you rewrite vols or correlation.' Then choose which number you would not show a treasurer without a footnote. A defensible stance: do not show raw parametric VaR alone if your backtests or sample show heavier tails—footnote that the normal model is ~2k lighter than historical on this book.

Trading Risk interview translation: you can compute both, explain the gap in dollars, and refuse to pretend they are interchangeable. That is more valuable than naming five vendor VaR engines. Keep the seed and both numbers in the notebook so a reviewer can rerun the claim in under a minute.

example.title: Footnote you would actually send
example.story: Draft: 'We show historical 99% 1-day VaR of ~29.4k on a 1,000,000 two-asset book (seeded lab). Parametric normal VaR is ~27.4k using z=2.326. We would not present the parametric number alone to a treasurer without stating the normal assumption and the ~2k gap to historical.'
example.takeaway: The footnote is part of the risk number; without it you implied false precision.

steps: Create a notebook or script week12_var.py. Use Python 3 with NumPy only for the core calc.
Set rng = numpy.random.default_rng(7).
Draw z = rng.standard_normal((250, 2)).

lessons.title: Expected shortfall versus VaR
body: Expected shortfall at level α (here 97.5%) means: take the losses worse than the α quantile of the loss distribution, and average those tail losses. If VaR is the curb, ES is how hard you hit the street after you jump it. Plain English: ES answers 'when we have a bad day past the cut, what is the typical loss on those days?' VaR alone is silent about severity beyond the cut.

Using the week-12 loss series, compute the 97.5% quantile of losses, select all losses at or above that quantile, and average them. Report that average as 97.5% ES in dollars on the same 1,000,000 book. Keep the series identical (seed 7 construction); otherwise you cannot compare to last week. Hull's ES section is the reading; the lab is the proof you understood the definition with numbers.

FRTB (Fundamental Review of the Trading Book) also cares about 97.5% and about P&L flavors—actual P&L (APL) and hypothetical P&L (HPL)—in supervisory backtesting and attribution. You are not implementing a full MAR32 stack this week; you are learning why supervisors talk about both the capital-style severity measure and the exception count used in traffic-light backtests.

example.title: ES from the seeded series
example.story: From week-12 losses (250 days), let q = quantile(losses, 0.975). ES = mean(losses[losses >= q]). That number will sit above the 97.5% VaR quantile by construction. Print q and ES side by side so you can show the gap between 'threshold' and 'average beyond threshold.'
example.takeaway: If you only quote VaR, you are silent about how severe the days past VaR are—that silence is what ES fills.

lessons.title: FRTB in plain English: SA, IMA, and why ES shows up
body: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) is the Basel market-risk capital rewrite most banks still implement in phases. Two calculation tracks matter in interviews and in Murex-adjacent work. The standardised approach (SA) maps positions into risk-factor buckets, applies prescribed risk weights and correlations, and adds a residual risk add-on where products do not fit cleanly. You do not need to memorise every bucket this week; you do need the sentence: SA is a rulebook charge driven by classification and weights, not by your internal VaR engine.

The internal models approach (IMA) lets a bank use approved internal expected shortfall models on modellable risk factors, with strict backtesting, P&L attribution (PLA), and a capital outcome that can jump when factors are deemed non-modellable (NMRF). That is why week-12 VaR and this week's ES/backtest lab are not academic toys for a Murex market-risk SME — they are the numerics behind the conversation when a desk asks why capital or limits moved after a methodology or market-data change.

Keep three artefacts in one notebook note: (1) the risk measure and horizon you computed, (2) the exception count / traffic light, (3) one line on what would break an IMA-style story (stale curve, missing risk factor, PLA fail). You are not filing a regulatory return; you are proving you can sit between the engine output and the governance question.

lessons.title: Exceptions, Kupiec, Christoffersen, traffic lights
body: A VaR exception occurs when realized loss exceeds the VaR number you published for that day. In the lab, use a single historical 99% VaR from the full sample as a teaching shortcut, or a simple rolling rule if you already built one—but be explicit which you used. Count exceptions over 250 days. At 99%, you expect about 2.5 exceptions in 250 days if the model is calibrated; more may still be green until you cross supervisory zones.

Kupiec's 1995 proportion-of-failures test (unconditional coverage) asks whether the observed exception rate matches the promised p (here 0.01). The likelihood-ratio statistic is compared to a chi-square critical value with 1 degree of freedom; at 95% confidence that critical value is 3.84. Christoffersen's 1998 test adds independence: exceptions should not clump. Remember chi-square 5.99 for 2 degrees of freedom at 95% when you combine coverage and independence. You do not need to memorize the algebra if you implement the formulas carefully once.

Classic Basel traffic-light zones for exceptions out of 250 days at 99%: 0–4 green, 5–9 amber, 10 or more red. Assign a zone from your count and show the count. Amber is not 'fine'; it is a supervisory conversation. Red is a model or process emergency.

example.title: Kupiec LR sketch with numbers
example.story: Suppose x exceptions in n=250 trials, p=0.01. The Kupiec LR statistic is -2 ln( [(1-p)^{n-x} p^x] / [(1-x/n)^{n-x} (x/n)^x] ) when 0<x<n. If x=3, the statistic is well below 3.84 → do not reject coverage at 95%. Traffic light: 3 is green. Print x, LR, critical value 3.84, and zone.
example.takeaway: Always publish the exception count next to the zone; the zone alone hides whether you were at 5 or at 9.

lessons.title: Why capital can use ES while backtests still count VaR exceptions
body: Capital wants a measure that reacts to the severity of the tail. ES does that: two portfolios can share a VaR yet differ in average loss beyond VaR, and ES separates them. That is why modern market-risk capital language emphasizes ES at high confidence (such as 97.5%). Saying 'we are fine because VaR is unchanged' can hide a nastier tail that only ES reveals.

Backtesting wants a crisp exception definition. Either today's loss breached the quantile forecast or it did not. That binary event feeds binomial-style tests (Kupiec) and independence tests (Christoffersen) and maps cleanly to traffic-light counts over 250 days. ES backtesting is possible but harder to communicate and standardize as a simple exception tally, so supervisory practice still leans on VaR exceptions for the day-count machinery even when capital uses ES.

Your ten-line note must say this in your own words: capital measure is not the same as backtest measure. State that you computed ES for capital-style severity and counted 99% VaR exceptions for backtest-style coverage. If you cannot explain that split, you are not ready to argue with a validator or a desk head about why a green traffic light can sit beside a rising ES.

example.title: One paragraph for a desk head
example.story: We use ES 97.5% to talk about how bad the bad days are for capital-style severity. We still count days beyond 99% VaR because that yes/no exception is what the Kupiec test and Basel traffic lights are built on. A green zone means exception frequency looks acceptable; it does not mean ES is low.
example.takeaway: Green traffic lights do not license you to ignore a rising ES.

weeks.goal: Implement EWMA and GARCH(1,1) next-day volatility on the same return series and state what a gap opening does to the forecast.
weeks.bigIdea: Volatility clustering means quiet days tend to follow quiet days and wild days tend to follow wild days. EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) updates variance by blending yesterday's variance with yesterday's squared return using a decay lambda. GARCH(1,1) adds a long-run level: next variance is a weighted mix of a constant, yesterday's squared return, and yesterday's variance. Correlation still enters through the covariance matrix when you move from one asset to a book—wrong correlation wrong risk, even if each vol is perfect.

lessons.title: EWMA volatility in one recursion
body: EWMA variance recursion in plain English: today's variance forecast equals λ times yesterday's variance forecast plus (1−λ) times yesterday's squared return. Lambda close to 1 (often 0.94 in RiskMetrics-style daily settings) means slow decay and long memory of shocks; smaller lambda means the forecast forgets faster. Next-day volatility is the square root of that variance forecast. Write the update once on paper with yesterday's numbers before you touch NumPy.

Use the same single-asset or portfolio return series you used in week 2 of the study plan. If that file is missing, rebuild a daily return series from the week-12 portfolio returns (pnl divided by book) so EWMA and GARCH sit on identical inputs. Initialize variance with the sample variance of the first window (for example first 20 days) or the full-sample variance—state which. Print the final next-day EWMA vol as a decimal and in percent so a desk reader does not guess units.

Jargon: return here means simple daily return (P&L over book), not log return, unless you explicitly choose logs and stay consistent. Squared return is the shock term that lifts variance after a big move. Handwriting the recursion catches index-off-by-one errors that notebooks hide, especially whether today's shock updates tomorrow's forecast.

example.title: One EWMA update
example.story: λ=0.94, yesterday variance forecast 0.00012, yesterday return −0.02 so squared return 0.0004. New variance = 0.94×0.00012 + 0.06×0.0004 = 0.0001368. New vol ≈ 1.17% daily.
example.takeaway: EWMA has no separate long-run mean; after a shock it only decays geometrically.

lessons.title: GARCH(1,1) and the long-run level
body: GARCH(1,1) variance recursion: next variance equals ω plus α times yesterday's squared return plus β times yesterday's variance. Plain English: a floor piece ω, a reaction α to the latest shock, and persistence β. Persistence α+β must be less than 1 for a stable long-run variance equal to ω divided by (1−α−β). If α+β is at or above 1, stop and fix parameters before you quote next-day vol to anyone.

Fit means choose ω, α, β. For this study week, a disciplined approach is: fix β around 0.9, α around 0.05, and set ω so that the long-run variance matches the sample variance of your series—or optimize with a simple grid search that maximizes Gaussian log-likelihood in NumPy. Do not add a specialized GARCH library unless you also keep a pure NumPy recursion that prints the same next-day vol. The graded object is the recursion you can read.

Print GARCH next-day vol beside EWMA vol on the same series. If they differ, explain which reacted more to the last few shocks. Correlation still matters for books: when you rebuild a two-asset covariance, a common teaching form is cov_ij,t = ρ_ij × σ_i,t × σ_j,t with slow-moving ρ. Updating vols but freezing a crisis ρ=0.9 is a classic Trading Risk footgun when markets calm.

example.title: Long-run variance check
example.story: Sample daily variance ≈ 0.000138. Choose α=0.05, β=0.90, then ω = 0.000138 × 0.05 = 0.0000069. After a quiet day GARCH drifts toward ~1.17% vol; after a shock it overshoots then mean-reverts.
example.takeaway: If α+β ≥ 1, your GARCH has no finite long-run variance—fix the parameters before you trust next-day vol.

lessons.title: Factor risk and a risk budget a PM can refuse
body: Buy-side portfolio risk is not only ‘vol went up.’ A portfolio manager thinks in factors and budgets: how much of the book’s risk is market beta, rates, credit, commodity, or a digital-asset factor you named yourself. Correlation matrices are the raw material; the deliverable is a risk-budget sentence.

Practical method inside this week’s hour: pick three synthetic sleeves (for example equity index, rates future, BTC). Estimate or assume pairwise correlations from your EWMA/GARCH work. Attribute variance with a simple one-factor or three-factor story — even a rough β to a market factor plus residual is enough if you write the assumptions.

Then write the budget: ‘We intend ~60% of standalone variance from market, ~25% from digital-asset idiosyncratic, ~15% from rates; a 10% overrun on digital-asset triggers a PM conversation, not a silent accept.’ That sentence is what buy-side risk owns.

example.title: Risk-budget challenge in the weekly meeting
example.story: Your three-sleeve book shows BTC vol spiking. The PM asks whether to cut BTC or hedge with the equity index. The factor view says BTC residual (not equity beta) drove the overrun — an equity hedge would fake comfort and leave the real risk. You propose trimming BTC 20% and leaving the index sleeve alone, with the budget line updated.
example.takeaway: Factor attribution decides the hedge. Hedging the wrong factor is how risk looks busy and still loses the PM’s trust.

lessons.title: Gap openings: what close-to-close GARCH cannot see
body: A gap opening is when the next open is far from the previous close—overnight news, a halt, a weekend macro print. A GARCH or EWMA forecast that only saw yesterday's close-to-close return cannot see that gap until the return that includes the gap enters the recursion. Intraday risk, open-auction risk, and jump risk sit outside the model state even when the printed next-day vol looks precise to two decimals.

Write half a page on this limitation in your own words. Name what the model cannot see (the open), what proxy you might add later (overnight return feature, separate overnight vol), and what a human should do when a gap is obvious (widen limits, cut size, demand a fresh mark). This is the week-14 write: not a survey paper, a crisp operational limitation a desk can act on before the open auction finishes.

Murex and FRTB practitioners already know vendor engines have overnight and intraday flavors. Your edge is stating the limitation before someone treats a close-to-close GARCH number as an all-hours guarantee. Put the words close-to-close model on any chart you show to Trading or Finance.

example.title: Weekend gap versus Friday forecast
example.story: Friday GARCH next-day vol prints 1.1% after a quiet +0.2% return. Sunday night the asset opens −6%. Monday open risk is not 1.1% until that gap enters the return; sizing to Friday's print under-risks the open.
example.takeaway: State 'close-to-close model' on the chart whenever you show GARCH to a trading audience.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo paths for a simple book
body: For a European-style factor move, a lognormal one-step or short multi-step simulation is enough: next price equals spot times exp((μ − 0.5σ²)Δt + σ√Δt Z) with Z a standard normal. For a one-day stress lab you can set μ=0 and work in return space with Δt as one trading day; be explicit. Five thousand paths is enough to stabilize a 95% loss for a teaching book if the generator is seeded and you print the seed next to the result.

Book choice that matches the plan: either short an option you can revalue with a simple Black–Scholes formula, or hold a crypto spot book such as 50 ETH at 3,000 and 1 BTC at 100,000 (synthetic). An ETH −30% style stress means you also inspect the loss when ETH drops 30% as a scenario benchmark beside the Monte Carlo cloud. That dumb scenario keeps the cloud honest when someone asks if 95% looks sane.

Report 95% loss (the 95% quantile of losses across paths) and expected shortfall beyond that quantile. Hull's Monte Carlo chapter for a European option is enough theory; you are not building a full XVA engine. Keep path count, seed, vols, and correlation in the printed header of the notebook output.

example.title: Synthetic ETH/BTC book
example.story: Spot ETH=3000, +50 ETH (150,000); BTC=100,000, +1 BTC (100,000). 5000 paths, ETH vol 5%, BTC vol 4%, ρ=0.7. Also print −30% ETH scenario loss = 45,000.
example.takeaway: Always park a dumb scenario number next to Monte Carlo so a Head of Risk can sanity-check the cloud.

lessons.title: Portfolio-level stress versus single-name scare charts
body: A single-name scare chart answers a newspaper question: what if ETH drops 30%. A portfolio-level stress answers a risk-committee question: after correlated moves, hedges, and financing, which sleeve pays. The second needs a book definition, a joint shock or factor path set, and a P&L bridge by sleeve — not a screenshot of one ticker.

When you run Monte Carlo paths, keep a sleeve tag on every revaluation. Print contribution to the 95% loss and to expected shortfall of losses. If one sleeve dominates, say so before you propose a hedge. If contributions flip when you change correlation, that is the finding — write it down before anyone debates the hedge ratio.

For buy-side and multi-asset paths, end with a PM sentence: dominant sleeve, proposed trim or hedge, and what you need confirmed (beta, borrow, venue depth). For Murex, add which risk factors in the engine must be alive for that sleeve contribution to be trustworthy, and which market-data feed would silently zero them.

lessons.title: From Monte Carlo paths to PFE-style exposure
body: Potential Future Exposure (PFE) asks a different question from market-risk VaR on a trading book. VaR asks how much mark-to-market you might lose. PFE asks how large a counterparty exposure might become along simulated market paths — typically a high quantile (often 95% or 99%) of the positive exposure distribution at a future date, sometimes summarised across a profile as effective EPE for capital storytelling.

You can build intuition without a full CCR engine. Simulate market factors, revalue the derivative or financed position on each path, take exposure as max(V, 0) after simple collateral rules if you have them, then read a quantile across paths at a chosen horizon. That number is PFE-like. Expected exposure (EE) is the mean of that positive exposure; EEPE aggregates EE over time with regulatory conventions you can name without implementing every Basel formula.

For the Murex path, write beside your Monte Carlo market-loss number a second line: exposure quantile at horizon T and whether collateral would have cut it. For the buy-side and tokenised paths, state who the counterparty is (PB, venue, custodian, chain settlement agent) because PFE without a counterparty noun is theatre.

lessons.title: Liquidity add-on that is not Almgren–Chriss
body: Liquidity add-on this week: cost equals half-spread times exit notional, plus an extra penalty when exit notional is greater than 5% of assumed daily volume (ADV). Example penalty: extra = exit_notional × impact_rate × (exit_notional/(0.05×ADV) − 1) when that ratio exceeds 1, else zero. Pick simple numbers and document them in comments. This is a spreadsheet control, not a market-impact research model.

Almgren–Chriss is a dynamic optimal-execution framework that balances temporary and permanent impact over a trading trajectory. You are not implementing that. Write in the notebook: 'Liquidity penalty is a half-spread plus size-versus-ADV add-on; not Almgren–Chriss.' Apply the penalty on any path whose exit size exceeds 5% of assumed volume—or apply it to all paths and separately flag the exceedances; state the rule in one line at the top of the lab.

Add the liquidity cost to the market loss to get total loss per path, then recompute 95% loss and ES. Show the dollar delta between market-only and market-plus-liquidity numbers. That delta is what you argue about with Treasury and Trading when size is large versus ADV. If the add-on never moves the 95% loss, say whether the book is tiny versus ADV or the penalty is too gentle.

example.title: Half-spread plus ADV breach
example.story: Exit notional 150,000; half-spread 10 bps → 150. ADV 2,000,000; 5% = 100,000; exit 1.5× cap; extra = 150,000×0.002×0.5 = 150; total add-on 300.
example.takeaway: If the add-on never moves the 95% loss, either the book is tiny versus ADV or your penalty is too gentle—say which.

lessons.title: Which number you show a Head of Risk
body: You now have week-12 VaR (historical about 29.4k on a separate 1,000,000 linear book) and a Monte Carlo stress loss on this week's book. They are not directly comparable unless you normalize books, horizons, and confidence levels. The write-up asks for one paragraph: which number you would show, and one caveat—not a table of every quantile you printed during debugging.

A defensible pattern: show the Monte Carlo 95% loss including liquidity when the question is stress-and-exit, and show week-12 VaR when the question is day-to-day statistical loss on the lab linear book. Do not mix them in one sentence without labeling horizons and books. Caveat examples: paths assume lognormal factors; liquidity is not Almgren–Chriss; seed dependence; correlation frozen at your chosen ρ.

Trading Risk credibility is choosing and labeling. A Head of Risk should leave your paragraph knowing the book, the confidence, and the one thing that would change the headline if it were false. That discipline matters more than showing both numbers and hoping they pick the right one in a noisy meeting. Write the paragraph as if it will be pasted into a risk pack cover note.

example.title: Paragraph skeleton
example.story: Show the 5,000-path 95% loss including liquidity for the ETH/BTC book when the question is stress-and-exit. Caveat: not Almgren–Chriss, and not one-for-one comparable to week-12 99% VaR on the 1,000,000 linear book.
example.takeaway: One headline number, one caveat, books and horizons named.

lab.goal: Run Monte Carlo stress with a liquidity add-on and print a separate PFE-style exposure quantile.
lab.why: Market loss, liquidity friction, and counterparty exposure are different management questions — especially on Murex CCR/XVA stacks.
steps: Create week15_mc_liquidity.py with numpy; set and print a fixed seed (for example 15).
Define book: eth_pos=50, eth_spot=3000, btc_pos=1, btc_spot=100000.
Draw 5000 correlated normals with ρ=0.7; apply vols 0.05 and 0.04; market_loss = -market_pnl.
Print scenario_loss_eth_m30 = 0.30 * eth_pos * eth_spot.
Compute liquidity_cost per path: half-spread times exit notional plus ADV penalty when exit > 5% of ADV; comment the formulas.
Print 95% loss and ES for market_loss and for total_loss = market_loss + liquidity_cost.
Print the sentence: Liquidity penalty is not Almgren-Chriss.
Print count of paths with exit > 5% of ADV.

Define exposure_t = max(value_t, 0) on each path at a chosen horizon (or at path end). Print pfe95 = quantile(exposure, 0.95) and counterparty_name. Do not add pfe95 into the market-loss total without a label.

Explicit not-Almgren–Chriss statement.
−30% ETH anchor, 5000 paths, and seed printed.

sessions.text: Read SR 11-7 lenses (purpose, conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis, ongoing monitoring). Add an FRTB-aware half-page: PLA, NMRF, desk evidence. Reuse week-13 ES/backtest outputs as exhibits.

Validation pack for the week-12 VaR, at most four pages: intended use, data, assumptions, limitations, challenger model (historical versus parametric), backtest result from week 13, monitoring metric, owner.

One signer’s page-1 expectation is logged.
weeks.goal: Write an SR 11-7-style validation pack for the week-12 VaR that also answers FRTB-aware questions (PLA, missing factors/NMRF, owners) in four pages or fewer.
weeks.bigIdea: Model risk management means treating models as things that can be wrong in costly ways, not as black boxes that mint truth. Federal Reserve SR 11-7 is supervisory guidance that expects purpose, conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis, and ongoing monitoring—among other practices. You are not becoming a validation team this week; you are writing a pack a validator could open without guessing your intent. Challenger models and named human owners are part of that honesty.

lessons.title: SR 11-7 lenses for a VaR you own
body: Read the Federal Reserve SR 11-7 letter on model risk management on the public federalreserve.gov site. Pull four lenses into your notes: purpose (why the model exists and what decision it supports), conceptual soundness (theory and implementation design), outcomes analysis (backtesting and benchmarking), and ongoing monitoring (what you watch after go-live). One-line jargon: model risk is the risk of loss from decisions made on wrong or misused model outputs. You need those four phrases ready in interviews and in pack headings.

Map those lenses to week-12 VaR without pretending this is a production capital engine. Purpose: daily statistical loss threshold for a linear two-asset teaching book—not capital finalization and not automated limit enforcement alone. Conceptual soundness: historical quantile versus normal parametric assumptions, Cholesky correlation, and seed 7 reproducibility. Outcomes analysis: week-13 exception count, Kupiec statistic, traffic-light zone, and expected shortfall. Monitoring: rolling exception rate and the dollar gap between historical and parametric VaR.

Resist scope creep. Four pages maximum. A validator skims; they do not want your autobiography. Every section should end with something checkable, such as a number, an owner role, or an explicit not-intended use. If a paragraph cannot be audited, it does not belong in the pack.

example.title: Purpose section that is narrow enough
example.story: Intended use: demonstrate 99% 1-day VaR on a synthetic 1,000,000 two-asset book for study evidence. Not intended: firm regulatory capital, automated liquidation, or client disclosure. Extending use requires new approval.
example.takeaway: A validation pack that claims every use is a pack that validates nothing.

lessons.title: IMA evidence: PLA, NMRF, and what a validator asks first
body: Under FRTB IMA, it is not enough to print ES. Supervisors and model risk care about P&L attribution (PLA): whether hypothetical and risk-theoretical P&L line up with the risk factors in the model. They care about non-modellable risk factors (NMRF) that attract stressed capital add-ons when data are too sparse. They care about desk-level eligibility and about whether the backtesting programme matches the capital story.

Your validation pack this week should therefore reserve a half-page for FRTB-aware questions even if your toy VaR is not an IMA candidate: Which P&L is used for exceptions? Which risk factors are missing from the engine mapping? What would a PLA fail look like in tickets (market data vs enrichment vs calc)? Who can freeze a limit when the traffic light turns amber?

For Trading Risk and Murex paths, translate each pack section into an owner: desk risk, market risk methodology, risk technology, model validation. One sentence each. If you cannot name an owner, the pack is not ready for a signer.

lessons.title: Pack contents: data, assumptions, challenger, owner
body: Build the pack with explicit headings: intended use; data; assumptions; limitations; challenger model; backtest result; monitoring metric; owner. Data must list seed 7, 250 by 2 normals, vols 1% and 2%, correlation 0.4, weights 60/40, and book 1,000,000, and must say the series is synthetic rather than market history. Assumptions include linear returns, constant vols for the parametric leg, and a teaching historical quantile on the sample window. Limitations include no options nonlinearity, no overnight gaps, and no production market-data feed.

Challenger model means a second method used to critique the primary one. Here the pair is historical versus parametric VaR. Report both numbers (about 29.4k versus 27.4k) and the gap in dollars. Backtest content should paste the week-13 exception count, Kupiec likelihood-ratio statistic, traffic-light zone, and 97.5% expected shortfall. Monitoring metric: pick one primary measure, for example a 20-day rolling exception count or the historical-minus-parametric gap. Owner: name a role, not only yourself as a student.

Add a short list of three decisions the model must not make alone, each with the human role that still decides—for example changing a desk limit, publishing external capital, or overriding a red traffic light. Those lines are as important as the VaR formula because they stop the pack from implying automation where judgment remains required.

example.title: Challenger table row
example.story: Primary historical 99% VaR ≈ 29,370. Challenger parametric ≈ 27,364 with z=2.326. Gap ≈ 2,006 (challenger lighter). Do not promote parametric alone without a footnote and owner sign-off.
example.takeaway: A challenger without a numeric gap is a slogan.

lessons.title: What signers read on page 1
body: People who sign model changes often read only page 1 under time pressure. Page 1 should contain intended use, material limitations, the challenger gap in dollars, the latest backtest traffic-light zone, the monitoring metric, the owner role, and the three reserved human decisions. Burying a red traffic light on page 4 is a governance failure dressed as thoroughness, and reviewers will treat it that way when something breaks in production.

Your industry ask this week is what one signer actually reads first. Log their answer in five lines and rearrange your pack if their page-1 list differs from yours. This is how study work turns into practitioner habits for Trading Risk and FRTB-adjacent conversations where platform numbers from systems like Murex meet model governance language from SR 11-7.

Keep tone factual. You are documenting a teaching model with production-grade structure, not claiming a certified bank model or a completed validation opinion. If a sentence sounds like marketing, cut it and replace it with a number, an owner, or a not-intended use that a reviewer can check without calling you afterward.

example.title: Page-1 box
example.story: Use: synthetic 99% 1-day VaR teaching model. Limitations: linear, synthetic data. Challenger gap ~2.0k. Backtest zone from week 13. Monitor rolling exceptions. Owner roles named. Reserved: limits, capital filing, red-zone override.
example.takeaway: If page 1 cannot be screenshotted into an email, it is too long.

weeks.title: Classify alerts: precision at a fixed recall

sessions.text: Classification metrics for a risk queue: precision, recall, false-positive rate, and the precision-recall curve. Accuracy is the wrong headline. Source: Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning, Ch. 3, or the scikit-learn precision-recall example. Write the definition of precision at 80% recall before you fit a model.

Synthetic alerts only, 200 rows you label yourself: true incident versus noise. Features: return z-score, volume multiple, hour of day, account concentration. Fit a regularized logistic regression. Report precision at recall 0.80, and the threshold that gets you there.
Name one feature a risk officer should reject as gameable or unstable. Say what a trader would do if that feature became the control.
Tell one risk officer, in writing, which feature you rejected and why. Log the reply.

criteria: Notebook reports precision at recall 0.80 and the probability threshold used.
The rejected feature is named, with the behavior a trader would use to game it.
One risk officer received that note, and the exchange is logged.
weeks.goal: Fit regularized logistic regression on 200 labeled synthetic alerts and report precision at recall 0.80 with the threshold used.
weeks.bigIdea: In a risk alert queue, accuracy is the wrong headline because true incidents are rare and missing one is costly. Recall is the fraction of true incidents you catch; precision is the fraction of your alerts that are real incidents. Precision at 80% recall means: set the score threshold so you catch 80% of true incidents, then measure how pure the resulting alert list is. Logistic regression gives a probability you can threshold; regularization shrinks coefficients to reduce overfitting on small synthetic sets.

lessons.title: Precision, recall, and why accuracy lies
body: Define the four counts used in alert queues: true positive (TP) means predicted incident and truly an incident; false positive (FP) means predicted incident but noise; false negative (FN) means predicted noise but was an incident; true negative (TN) means predicted noise and truly noise. Recall equals TP divided by (TP+FN). Precision equals TP divided by (TP+FP). False-positive rate equals FP divided by (FP+TN). Accuracy equals (TP+TN) divided by all rows, and it can look excellent if you always predict noise in a 95% noise queue while missing every incident.

Write the definition of precision at 80% recall before you fit anything. Sort alerts by model score descending, move the probability threshold until recall first reaches at least 0.80, then compute precision at that threshold. If several thresholds achieve recall of at least 0.80, pick the one with best precision, or the highest threshold that still meets recall, and state which rule you used so a reviewer can reproduce the number.

Sources for study include Géron Hands-On Machine Learning chapter 3 or the scikit-learn precision-recall examples. The Trading Risk translation is blunt: a desk will forgive some noise in the queue, but they will not forgive a silent miss on a true incident if your operating model claimed high recall.

example.title: Precision at recall 0.80 on a tiny grid
example.story: 20 true incidents in 200 rows. Recall 0.80 needs at least 16 catches. At threshold 0.35 with 16 TP and 24 FP, precision = 16/40 = 0.40. At 0.50 with only 12 TP, recall is 0.60 and fails the target.
example.takeaway: State the recall target first; precision is the cost you pay to hit it.

lessons.title: Synthetic alerts and regularized logistic regression
body: Build 200 synthetic alert rows you label yourself. Features should include return z-score (how many standard deviations the return is from a baseline), volume multiple (today's volume over typical volume), hour of day from 0 to 23, and account concentration (largest name or sector weight in the account). Label y=1 for true incident and y=0 for noise. Invent labels with a rule you write down in comments, for example making high z-score plus high concentration more often an incident, so the task is learnable but still noisy.

Fit regularized logistic regression with scikit-learn LogisticRegression using an L2 penalty. Use a stratified train/test split such as 140/60, or cross-validation, and report test-set precision at recall 0.80 so you are not grading yourself on training luck. Print the probability threshold that achieves recall of at least 0.80 on the evaluation set and the precision at that threshold.

Jargon in one line each: logistic regression models the log-odds of the incident class as a linear function of features; regularization adds a penalty on large coefficients so the fit cannot memorize noise on a small set. Treat the score as a ranking tool for a human queue, not as an autonomous block on trading, and do not let it become a hard control without maker-checker.

example.title: Minimal feature row
example.story: Row 87: z=3.1, volume_multiple=2.4, hour=14, concentration=0.55, label=1. Row 88: z=0.2, volume_multiple=1.1, hour=3, concentration=0.10, label=0. After fit, scores might be 0.82 versus 0.05; threshold 0.30 keeps 87 and drops 88.
example.takeaway: If you cannot explain a row's label in one sentence, your synthetic set is too cute to learn from.

lessons.title: Reject a gameable feature
body: Name one feature a risk officer should reject as gameable or unstable. Gameable means a trader can change the feature without reducing economic risk—for example splitting an account to lower measured concentration while keeping the same economic exposure across legal entities. Unstable means the feature's meaning changes with calendar effects or vendor feed quirks, such as hour-of-day when the market-data feed is delayed and timestamps no longer mean what the model assumes.

Say what a trader would do if that feature became the control. Then tell one risk officer in writing which feature you rejected and why. The point is governance of machine-learning features in risk workflows: models inherit incentives, and desks learn the scoring function faster than documentation admits when silence is rewarded.

Keep the rejected feature out of your production story even if it helped the toy metric on synthetic rows. Precision at recall 0.80 on synthetic data is practice; shipping a gameable control is how you lose the desk's trust and teach people to optimize the score instead of the underlying risk they were hired to manage.

example.title: Concentration split game
example.story: If account concentration alone gates escalation, a trader books two accounts at 40% instead of one at 80% and your feature falls asleep while economic risk is unchanged.
example.takeaway: Ask how you would game the feature if your bonus depended on silence before you celebrate precision.

lab.goal: 200-row synthetic alert classifier with precision at recall 0.80 and the threshold printed.
lab.why: Queue models must be judged on the recall target operations actually needs.
steps: Create week17_alert_classifier.py using numpy/pandas/sklearn.
Set seed 17. Generate 200 rows: zscore, volume_multiple, hour, concentration.
Assign labels with a written probabilistic rule in comments; print class balance (aim roughly 15–30% incidents).
Stratified train/test split. Fit LogisticRegression(penalty='l2', max_iter=1000).
On the test set, sweep probability thresholds from 0.01 to 0.99.
Find threshold where recall >= 0.80 (state tie-break: best precision among those). Print threshold, recall, precision.
If recall never reaches 0.80, adjust the label rule or features and rerun, or document the failure clearly.
Write week17_rejected_feature.md naming one rejected feature and the gaming behavior.
expected: Printed precision at recall 0.80 and the probability threshold.
Class balance and seed printed.
Rejected-feature note with the gaming behavior.

weeks.title: Anomalies, then a human close-out

sessions.text: Median absolute deviation versus isolation forest. Write down when an unlabeled method is honest, and when it only rediscovers a holiday or a corporate action. A survey paper is unnecessary.
Run MAD and sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest on the same synthetic series. Print the top 10 dates from each. Mark which dates both methods flag.
Investigation card: the five fields an investigator sees, the action that closes the alert, and the action that escalates it. No free-text-only close.
Ask one team how they measure false positives today. Record the formula. If they have no formula, write that sentence down.

criteria: Top 10 dates from both detectors are printed, and the overlap is marked.
The investigation card has a structured close reason, not only a comment box.
A real false-positive formula, or the absence of one, is logged.
weeks.goal: Compare MAD and IsolationForest on one synthetic series, mark overlaps, and design an investigation card with a structured close.
weeks.bigIdea: Anomaly detection flags unusual points without needing a label for every past incident. Median absolute deviation (MAD) is a robust spread measure: points far from the median relative to MAD look like outliers under a simple z-score. IsolationForest is a tree ensemble that isolates points that are easy to separate from the rest of the sample. Unlabeled methods are honest when you treat them as hypotheses for humans; they are dishonest when you pretend every holiday or corporate action they rediscover is fraud. The close-out must be structured so the queue learns.

lessons.title: MAD versus IsolationForest
body: MAD means median absolute deviation: the median of absolute distances from the series median. A common robust z-score is 0.6745 times (x minus median) divided by MAD, using the Gaussian consistency constant found in many textbooks. Flag the top 10 days by absolute robust z-score. This method is transparent and fast; it struggles when anomalies are multivariate patterns rather than extreme values on a single column.

IsolationForest from sklearn.ensemble builds random partitions of the feature space; anomalies tend to need fewer partitions to isolate from the rest of the sample. You get an anomaly score per point; print the top 10 dates by that score. The method can catch odd combinations across features if you feed more than one column, but it is sensitive to the contamination setting and can excitedly flag seasonality or calendar structure that is not a risk incident.

Run both detectors on the same synthetic series. Mark which dates appear in both top-10 lists. Agreement is a stronger investigation hint than a single method screaming alone. Disagreement is also informative: MAD-only spikes may be univariate extremes that IsolationForest down-ranks when other features still look normal.

example.title: Overlap set
example.story: Series of 180 days with planted spikes on days 40, 91, 150, plus flat holiday day 60. MAD top 10 includes those four; IsolationForest top 10 includes the three spikes plus two choppy days. Overlap = {40, 91, 150}.
example.takeaway: Score the overlap set first; treat single-method flags as second-tier.

lessons.title: When unlabeled methods are honest
body: Unlabeled methods are honest when your question is what looks unlike the recent distribution and a human investigates with context before anyone is blamed. They are not honest when used as automatic blame: a corporate action, index rebalance, or market holiday can look anomalous and still be completely correct. Write that rule down before you demo scores to a desk that is already tired of false pages and noisy queues.

For Trading Risk, anomaly scores should open an investigation card, not auto-file a breach or auto-block trading. Tie this week to the week-10 paging philosophy: platform pages are numeric and owned, while desk investigations need structured outcomes so metrics like false-positive rate become computable instead of vibes repeated in a standup meeting nobody can audit later.

Skip survey papers for this week. Your study product is the comparison table plus the investigation card design. If a method only rediscovers holidays, say so in the lab output next to the date rather than hiding the artifact in a discussion section nobody reads when the pager fires at two in the morning.

example.title: Holiday rediscovered
example.story: IsolationForest flags a near-zero volume flat session that is a market holiday in your synthetic calendar. Closing as INCIDENT poisons labels; closing as EXPECTED_CALENDAR with a reason code keeps the queue clean.
example.takeaway: If your detector cannot be wrong in a documented way, you will teach it to be loudly wrong.

lessons.title: Investigation card with structured close
body: Design an investigation card: the five fields an investigator sees, the action that closes the alert, and the action that escalates it. No free-text-only close is allowed under any circumstance. Structured close means a controlled reason code plus an optional comment—for example EXPECTED_MARKET, FEED_ERROR, TRUE_INCIDENT, DUPLICATE, or NEEDS_MORE_DATA—not a blank box that becomes a novel and cannot be aggregated for weekly reporting.

Suggested five fields: (1) alert id and timestamp, (2) entity such as account, book, or instrument, (3) detector votes including MAD rank, IsolationForest rank, and overlap yes or no, (4) key metrics snapshot such as return, volume, and concentration, and (5) evidence links such as mark source and last parameter version. Close action sets status CLOSED with a reason code. Escalate action sets status ESCALATED to desk or platform on-call with a severity.

This card is how week-17 precision and recall become measurable in real operations: without structured closes you cannot compute false positives in a way that survives staff turnover. Your industry ask is the team's false-positive formula, or the honest sentence that they currently have none.

example.title: Close record
example.story: Alert A-1842 closed as FEED_ERROR after a 90-second BTC mark spike; MAD rank 1; IF rank 2; overlap yes; evidence = market-data incident INC-339. Comment optional; reason code is what reporting counts.
example.takeaway: If close reasons are free text only, your false-positive rate is a vibe.

weeks.title: RAG over your own memos, with a refusal

sessions.text: AI-engineer retrieval block: chunk size, overlap, embeddings, and why an answer must cite a chunk. Read the definitions of faithfulness and response relevancy in the RAGAS docs (docs.ragas.io). You will score by hand this week. Do not index employer documents, client names, or live thresholds.
Index only memos you wrote in weeks 1–8. Ask: why was the threshold 5% rather than 3%? The answer must quote the week-4 memo. Keep the index local.
Write one question the system must refuse because the memos do not contain the fact. Show the refusal.
In six lines, describe the prototype to one engineer. Ask which data they would never put in the index. Log the answer.

criteria: The threshold answer quotes the week-4 memo, and the quoted sentence is visible in the output.
One out-of-corpus question is refused, and the refusal is saved.
An engineer’s do-not-index list is logged. No employer data is in the index.
weeks.goal: Build a local retrieval system over only your weeks 1–8 study memos so answers cite real chunks, quote the week-4 threshold memo, refuse what is not in the corpus, and never touch employer data.
weeks.bigIdea: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means the model answers from documents you give it, not from guesswork. For risk work, that only helps if every claim can be traced to a chunk you own, and if the system says "I do not have that" when the memos are silent. This week you index only your own early-plan writing, keep the index on your machine, and practice one forced refusal so silence becomes a feature, not a failure.

lessons.title: What RAG is, in risk language
body: A plain chatbot invents when it does not know. A retrieval-augmented generation system, usually called RAG, first searches a small library of text you prepared, pulls the best matching passages, and then drafts an answer that must lean on those passages. In risk language, the library is your control memory: threshold memos, metric definitions, and ownership notes you already wrote. Without retrieval, the model guesses from general training, which is useless when the question is why your band is five percent rather than three. With retrieval, every sentence can be pointed back to a chunk you own and can open on disk.

Chunk size is how many words or characters you cut each memo into. Overlap is a short shared strip between neighboring chunks so a sentence that straddles a cut is not lost. Embeddings turn each chunk into a numeric fingerprint so similar meaning can be found even when the wording differs. Faithfulness means the answer stays true to the retrieved text and does not smuggle in extra facts. Response relevancy means the answer addresses the question asked. Score both by hand: if a sentence cannot be pointed to a chunk, it does not belong, no matter how polished it sounds.

Hard privacy rule for this entire AI block: index only memos you wrote in weeks one through eight of this plan. Do not index employer documents, client names, live risk thresholds, desk books, or anything marked confidential. If you are unsure whether a file is personal study material, leave it out. Keep the index local. A smaller clean corpus beats a larger dirty one, because one leaked production number ruins the exercise for a risk professional.

example.title: Chunking a threshold memo
example.story: Your week-4 memo is about 600 words with headings for decision, metric, loss if too wide, alert volume if too tight, owner, evidence to change the number, and rollback. You split it into overlapping 200-word chunks. The sentence "We keep the band at 5% rather than 3% because a 3% band would fire on routine overnight gaps and bury the desk in noise" lands fully inside one chunk. When someone later asks why 5% not 3%, retrieval should surface that chunk first so the answer can quote it instead of inventing a reason.
example.takeaway: Chunk so the decision sentence survives intact; then force the answer to quote that sentence.

lessons.title: Citations are the control, not decoration
body: In a risk workflow, an uncited AI answer is an uncontrolled opinion. Your prototype must show the quoted text from the source memo in the output, not only a file name or a vague see-threshold-memo reference. Prefer a short verbatim quote over a paraphrase when the question is about a specific threshold, owner, rollback rule, or alert-volume argument. Paraphrase is fine for teaching tone; it is dangerous for control language, because a single wrong percentage can look authoritative and still be false. Make the quote visible in the same screen or log line as the answer.

Design the prompt with three hard rules: answer only from the retrieved chunks; if the chunks do not contain the fact, refuse; always include the quote. That instruction is part of the control design, the same way a limit system states who can approve a breach. Human override stays with you. If the quote looks wrong, if the chunk is stale after you edited the memo, or if retrieval pulled the wrong heading, discard the answer and fix the index or the source file. Never let a smooth paragraph override a memo you can open and read.

Treat citation format as a mini standard. A good pattern is: state the claim, open a quote from the week-four memo, then name the filename and heading. If two chunks disagree because you revised a memo and forgot to re-index, stop, rebuild, and re-ask. The deliverable is proof that a threshold question returns a sentence you can verify against the original memo, and that you know how to kill an answer that fails that test.

example.title: Good citation versus smooth invention
example.story: Question: "Why was the threshold 5% rather than 3%?" Bad answer: "Five percent is industry standard for crypto liquidations" with no quote. Good answer: "According to the week-4 threshold memo: 'We keep the band at 5% rather than 3% because a 3% band would fire on routine overnight gaps and bury the desk in noise.' Owner: Head of Market Risk. Rollback: revert to prior band if alert volume exceeds the stated weekly cap." The second answer is usable in a study portfolio because a reviewer can open the memo and verify the sentence.
example.takeaway: If the quote is not visible in the output, the citation failed.

lessons.title: Forced refusal and the do-not-index list
body: A useful risk RAG system refuses when the corpus does not support an answer. That is not a product bug; it is the boundary for what the tool is allowed to know. Write at least one question that your weeks one through eight memos cannot answer—for example a live firm limit, a client name, or an unpublished parameter—and require a clear refusal. Soft hedges such as it might be around five percent are failures. The refusal should say the fact is not in the indexed memos and that the system will not invent a live threshold or client detail.

Before you demo to anyone, ask an engineer which classes of data they would never put in the index. Expect answers like production books, personal data, unpublished model parameters, raw order logs, and anything under legal hold. Log that list next to your prototype so the privacy stance is written, not assumed. Your six-line description should mention local index, study memos only, citation requirement, and refusal behavior. Ask which data they would never allow, not whether the demo looks impressive.

Forced refusal also trains you as the operator. When the system refuses correctly, do not argue it into answering. When it answers a question it should have refused, mark that as a failure and fix prompts or retrieval filters. Keep the out-of-corpus question and the refusal text beside the successful threshold quote. Together they show grounded speech when the memo supports the fact, and silence when it does not. No employer data enters the index while you practice either mode.

example.title: One question that must fail closed
example.story: You ask: "What is our firm's current BTC maintenance-margin rate for tier 3?" Your index only has study memos with synthetic tiers. The system replies: "I do not have that fact in the indexed memos. I will not invent a live firm threshold." You save that refusal screenshot or log line as a deliverable. Separately, an engineer tells you never to index raw order logs or customer identifiers; you write those two items into a six-line note.
example.takeaway: A saved refusal plus a do-not-index list proves you built a bounded tool, not a leaky search box.

Build or run a local vector index (or a simple keyword index if embeddings are unavailable). Do not upload the corpus to a shared third-party store that retains your files for training.
Ask the system: "Why was the threshold 5% rather than 3%?" Require the answer to include a verbatim quote from the week-4 threshold memo.
Confirm the quoted sentence appears in the output and that you can open the week-4 file and find the same sentence.

Write a six-line description of the prototype for an engineer and ask which data they would never put in the index. Log their answer.
